topic_tag: wolves and a wintering elk herd
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Over the decade that followed, the pack ______ the herd.

worlds.passage: When wolves returned to a mountain valley in 1995, a pack of nine settled along the creek where a herd of four hundred elk spends each winter. Over the decade that followed, the pack ______ the herd. The elk it killed were mostly old cows and lame calves, and their carcasses lay scattered across the open benches in every direction, often two miles from the willow thickets where the herd had been feeding that morning. The herd spent its evenings in those thickets, and its calves were born there each spring.
worlds.explanation: "Chased" fits: the wolves took the slowest elk, old cows and lame calves, and the carcasses lay up to two miles from where the herd had been feeding, so the wolves ran elk down until the weakest fell behind. "Ambushed" fails because an attack from hiding takes whatever elk passes the hiding place, at close range; these kills fell on open benches far from the herd's feeding ground and picked out the weakest, which is what a pursuit does. "Corralled" fails because the carcasses lay in every direction, so the wolves were not driving the herd into any one place. "Cowed" fails because the herd kept spending its evenings in the thickets and calving there, so the wolves did not frighten it out of its habits.

ambushed.quote: scattered across the open benches in every direction
ambushed.why: kills on open ground far from where the herd fed, chosen by weakness
ambushed.surface_fit: wolves are often described lying in wait, and a pack settled along the creek where the elk winter suggests a hidden attack
ambushed.inference: a predator striking from cover kills whatever passes its hiding place, close by; carcasses spread over open benches two miles from the morning's feeding ground, almost all old or lame, are the end of runs that the slowest lost

corralled.why: no single place where the herd was driven
corralled.surface_fit: a pack of nine working a herd together suggests driving the elk into a trap, a familiar picture of pack hunting
corralled.inference: if the kills lay in every direction across the benches, each hunt ended wherever a straggler fell, so the wolves were not pushing the herd toward any confining place

cowed.quote: its calves were born there each spring
cowed.why: the herd kept using the thickets
cowed.surface_fit: the return of wolves is widely reported to have frightened elk out of creekside willows
cowed.inference: a herd that spends its evenings in the thickets and drops its calves there each spring, with the wolves living along the same creek, has not been frightened out of its habits

worlds.passage: When wolves returned to a mountain valley in 1995, a pack of nine settled along the creek where a herd of four hundred elk spends each winter. Over the decade that followed, the pack ______ the herd. Collars showed the wolves spending their days in the creek's willow thickets where the herd's trails cross it. Nearly every carcass lay on one of those trails within a few yards of the water, and the dead included prime bulls as often as old cows. Each evening the herd filed down from the open benches along the same trails to drink, and the willows beside them were cropped to knee height.
worlds.explanation: "Ambushed" fits: the wolves lay all day in thickets at the trail crossings, the herd came down those trails every evening, and the kills fell right there, so the wolves waited hidden for the elk to come to them. "Chased" fails because the kills lay within yards of the thickets and took prime bulls as often as old cows; a pursuit ends far off and takes the slowest. "Corralled" fails because the herd walked down to the crossings on its own each evening, so nothing drove it there. "Cowed" fails because the herd kept filing down the very trails where it lost animals and cropping the willows beside them.

chased.quote: prime bulls as often as old cows
chased.why: kills at the thicket edge took strong and weak alike
chased.surface_fit: wolves are best known as pursuit hunters, so chased is the obvious verb for a pack and a herd
chased.inference: a chase is lost by the slowest animal and ends wherever it falls behind; kills within yards of the thickets that take prime bulls as often as old cows came from close-range strikes, not runs

corralled.quote: Each evening the herd filed down from the open benches
corralled.why: the elk came to the spot by themselves
corralled.surface_fit: a pack picking the spot where its prey gathers sounds like hemming the herd into a trap
corralled.inference: the herd walked down its own trails to drink every evening while the wolves lay in the thickets, so the pack moved nothing; the elk came to the place themselves

cowed.quote: the willows beside them were cropped to knee height
cowed.why: the elk kept feeding at the dangerous crossings
cowed.surface_fit: wolves returning to a valley are widely said to have frightened elk away from creeks
cowed.inference: elk that file down the trails where they are killed and crop the willows beside them to knee height are still feeding at the crossings, so fear has not changed where they go

worlds.passage: When wolves returned to a mountain valley in 1995, a pack of nine settled along the creek where a herd of four hundred elk spends each winter. Over the decade that followed, the pack ______ the herd. In deep snow the wolves spread out in a wide arc on the open benches and walked slowly toward the elk, which moved off ahead of them downhill into a side canyon where drifts lay chest-deep; there, floundering, several fell in an afternoon to wolves trotting on the crust. By spring the elk were back grazing the benches and the willows along the creek.
worlds.explanation: "Corralled" fits: walking in a wide arc, the wolves pushed the elk ahead of them into a canyon of chest-deep drifts, a confined place where they could not escape. "Chased" fails because the wolves walked slowly and the elk moved off ahead of them, so the kills came from where the elk were pushed, not from outrunning them. "Ambushed" fails because the wolves came at the herd in the open, spread across the benches in plain sight, instead of waiting hidden. "Cowed" fails because by spring the elk were back on the benches and in the creek willows, so the pack did not frighten them out of their range.

chased.why: the wolves walked; the elk moved ahead and were trapped by the drifts, not run down
chased.surface_fit: the wolves trot on the crust and the elk move away from them, which reads at first like a pursuit
chased.inference: wolves walking slowly in an arc push the elk ahead rather than overtaking them, and the elk died only once the canyon drifts held them, so position, not pursuit, decided the hunt

ambushed.quote: spread out in a wide arc on the open benches
ambushed.why: the wolves approached in open view rather than lying hidden
ambushed.surface_fit: elk dying in a side canyon sounds like a trap sprung on them, which is what an ambush is
ambushed.inference: a line of wolves walking across open benches is visible to the elk the whole time, and the elk moved away from it, so the attack did not come from concealment

cowed.quote: back grazing the benches and the willows
cowed.why: the elk resumed their old range by spring
cowed.surface_fit: the frightening effect of wolves on elk is famous, so cowed fits both the topic and the sentence
cowed.inference: if the elk return to the same benches and creek willows once the snow goes, the pack has not changed where they live or feed, so they were not intimidated

worlds.passage: When wolves returned to a mountain valley in 1995, a pack of nine settled along the creek where a herd of four hundred elk spends each winter. Over the decade that followed, the pack ______ the herd. It killed fewer than thirty elk a year, most of them on the open benches above the creek. Elk that once grazed for hours in the willow thickets began to pass through them without stopping, heads up, even when collars placed the pack thirty miles off, and fed in scattered bands on the benches, lifting their heads every few bites. By 2005 willows long held to knee height stood taller than a rider.
worlds.explanation: "Cowed" fits: the pack killed few elk, yet the herd stopped lingering in the thickets, stayed watchful while feeding, and kept doing so even when the wolves were thirty miles off, so the wolves changed the herd's behavior through fear. "Chased" fails because the elk avoided the thickets in weeks when no wolf was near them, so no pursuit was pushing them out. "Ambushed" fails because most kills were on the open benches, away from the thickets that could have hidden a wolf. "Corralled" fails because the elk fed in scattered bands across the benches, so they were spread out rather than confined.

chased.quote: even when collars placed the pack thirty miles off
chased.why: the elk kept avoiding the thickets with no wolves anywhere near
chased.surface_fit: the elk moved out of the willow thickets onto the benches, which looks like being driven out by wolves, and chasing is what wolves are known for
chased.inference: elk that trot through the thickets while the pack is thirty miles away are not being pursued at that moment, so their move to the benches comes from fear, not from being run off

ambushed.quote: most of them on the open benches
ambushed.why: kills happened on open ground, not at the thickets
ambushed.surface_fit: elk avoiding dense willows is what one would expect if wolves were lying in wait there, so ambushed is a natural guess
ambushed.inference: if most kills fell on the open benches, away from the thickets where a wolf could hide, the pack was not killing from cover

corralled.why: the herd spread out across the benches
corralled.surface_fit: a pack and a herd suggest wolves herding elk together into one place, so corralled fits the sentence
corralled.inference: a herd split into scattered bands across open benches has been dispersed, not gathered into a confined place, so the wolves did not pen it

topic_tag: voles in a grass strip beside a rail line
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Two decades of trapping suggest that the strip has served as the voles' ______.

worlds.passage: Beside a rail line, a strip of uncut grass runs twelve miles across plowed farmland past small woodlots, and meadow voles live in both the strip and the woodlots. Two decades of trapping suggest that the strip has served as the voles' ______. Most voles caught in the strip are young, few are caught twice at the same spot, and a vole marked in one woodlot was trapped the next year in another nine miles along the line. Woodlots beside the strip now share the same variants of a gene, while woodlots as far apart across the bare fields each carry their own.
worlds.explanation: "Corridor" fits: young voles keep moving through the strip, one reached a woodlot nine miles along it, and woodlots linked by the strip share gene variants that equally distant woodlots across the fields do not, so the strip carries voles between woodlots. "Cage" fails because voles are rarely caught twice in one place and travel miles along it, so it does not hold them. "Cafeteria" fails because the voles in it are moving on to other woodlots, not making trips out to feed and returning home. "Cemetery" fails because the young voles passing through it go on to breed in distant woodlots, as the shared genes show, so it is not where they die.

cage.quote: few are caught twice at the same spot
cage.why: voles keep moving and reach distant woodlots
cage.surface_fit: a narrow strip boxed in by plowed fields on both sides sounds like an enclosure that hems voles in
cage.inference: voles that are seldom caught twice in one place, one of which reached a woodlot nine miles away, move freely along and out of the strip, so it does not confine them

cafeteria.quote: trapped the next year in another nine miles along the line
cafeteria.why: voles end up in other woodlots instead of returning home
cafeteria.surface_fit: voles from woodlots going out into a strip of uncut grass invites the idea that they go there to feed
cafeteria.inference: a vole that leaves one woodlot and settles in another nine miles away is traveling, and the shared genes show many have done so; a feeding place is visited from home and left again

cemetery.quote: now share the same variants of a gene
cemetery.why: voles crossing the strip survive to breed in the woodlots they reach
cemetery.surface_fit: a thin strip of grass beside a railway sounds dangerous for small animals, so a place where they die is a natural guess
cemetery.inference: genes can spread between woodlots along the strip only if the young voles moving through it live to breed at the far end, so the strip is not killing them

worlds.passage: Beside a rail line, a strip of uncut grass runs twelve miles across plowed farmland past small woodlots, and meadow voles live in both the strip and the woodlots. Two decades of trapping suggest that the strip has served as the voles' ______. Voles born in the strip feed and nest there all their lives: of thousands marked, none has been trapped more than half a mile from where it was first caught, though woodlots lie a few hundred yards off across fields left bare all winter. Over two decades each stretch of the strip has come to carry its own variants of a gene, unlike the nearest woodlot's voles.
worlds.explanation: "Cage" fits: the strip's voles never move more than half a mile, although woodlots lie a few hundred yards off across bare fields, and each stretch has drifted genetically on its own, so the strip holds its voles in place. "Corridor" fails because nothing travels along it; gene variants differ from one stretch to the next. "Cafeteria" fails because the voles that feed in the strip were born and live there and differ genetically from the woodlot voles, so woodlot voles are not coming in to eat. "Cemetery" fails because each stretch has bred its own gene variants over two decades, which takes generations of voles living long enough to breed there.

corridor.quote: more than half a mile from where it was first caught
corridor.why: no vole moves far, and genes differ stretch by stretch
corridor.surface_fit: a twelve-mile strip of grass across farmland is the textbook picture of a wildlife corridor
corridor.inference: if no marked vole moves more than half a mile and each stretch carries its own gene variants, voles are not passing along the strip

cafeteria.why: the strip's feeders are residents, genetically distinct from woodlot voles
cafeteria.surface_fit: the voles feed in a grass strip lying a few hundred yards from woodlots full of voles, which suggests a place woodlot voles come out to eat
cafeteria.inference: the voles feeding in the strip were born there and carry gene variants the nearest woodlot's voles lack, so the woodlot voles are not coming in to feed; the strip is the residents' whole range

cemetery.quote: each stretch of the strip has come to carry its own variants
cemetery.why: generations have lived and bred there
cemetery.surface_fit: small animals hemmed into a narrow strip beside a railway sound doomed, so a place of death is tempting
cemetery.inference: local gene variants build up over two decades only through generation after generation of voles surviving to breed in each stretch, so the strip is not where they die off

worlds.passage: Beside a rail line, a strip of uncut grass runs twelve miles across plowed farmland past small woodlots, and meadow voles live in both the strip and the woodlots. Two decades of trapping suggest that the strip has served as the voles' ______. Marked voles from the woodlots are caught in the strip after dark, among grass stems clipped of their seed heads, and back in their own woodlots by morning, never more than a few hundred yards from home. They nest only in the woodlots, and woodlots the strip touches hold more voles each spring than woodlots it does not.
worlds.explanation: "Cafeteria" fits: woodlot voles come into the strip at night, where stems are clipped of their seed heads, and are home by morning, so they use it as a place to feed. "Corridor" fails because each vole goes back to its own woodlot and stays within a few hundred yards of it, so none travels along the strip. "Cage" fails because the voles leave it every morning and nest in the woodlots. "Cemetery" fails because woodlots the strip touches hold more voles each spring, so the nightly visits help the voles rather than killing them.

corridor.quote: back in their own woodlots by morning
corridor.why: each vole returns home rather than moving along the strip
corridor.surface_fit: a strip of grass running past woodlots is the textbook wildlife corridor, and voles are entering it from the woodlots
corridor.inference: voles that are back in their own woodlot by morning and never go more than a few hundred yards from it are not using the strip to move between woodlots

cage.quote: They nest only in the woodlots
cage.why: the voles leave daily and live elsewhere
cage.surface_fit: a narrow strip hemmed in by plowed fields sounds like a pen that could trap animals inside it
cage.inference: animals that nest in the woodlots and return there each morning come and go freely, so the strip does not hold them

cemetery.why: the visits leave the woodlots better stocked
cemetery.surface_fit: small animals venturing into an open strip beside a railway at night sounds dangerous, so a place where they die is tempting
cemetery.inference: if woodlots whose voles visit the strip hold more voles each spring than woodlots without it, the visits add to the voles' numbers, so the strip is not where they die

worlds.passage: Beside a rail line, a strip of uncut grass runs twelve miles across plowed farmland past small woodlots, and meadow voles live in both the strip and the woodlots. Two decades of trapping suggest that the strip has served as the voles' ______. Young voles pushed out of crowded woodlots each spring settle in the strip's seed-heavy grass within a few hundred yards of where they entered, and owls hunt it from the line's poles. Within a month, tags of over half the voles marked there turn up in pellets beneath the poles, while those that wander back to a woodlot breed there the next spring.
worlds.explanation: "Cemetery" fits: young voles settle in the strip, and owls hunting from the poles kill more than half of them there within a month, so the strip is where the voles die. "Corridor" fails because the voles stop within a few hundred yards of where they enter and are killed there within weeks, so they do not pass along it. "Cage" fails because voles can wander back to a woodlot, so the strip does not hold them in. "Cafeteria" fails because, although the voles feed on its seed, over half of them are killed there by owls within a month, so what the strip mainly does to them is kill them, not feed them.

corridor.quote: within a few hundred yards of where they entered
corridor.why: the young voles stop near where they enter and are killed there
corridor.surface_fit: young animals pushed out of crowded ground into a strip that links woodlots is exactly how wildlife corridors are said to work
corridor.inference: voles that settle within a few hundred yards of where they entered and are eaten within a month never travel the strip to other woodlots

cage.surface_fit: animals that enter a strip and mostly never come out sound trapped, so an enclosure is a tempting metaphor
cage.inference: since voles can and do wander back to a woodlot and breed there, the strip does not confine them; most fail to return because owls kill them

cafeteria.quote: tags of over half the voles marked there turn up in pellets
cafeteria.why: the decisive fact is that most voles in the strip are killed there
cafeteria.surface_fit: the strip's grass is seed-heavy and the voles live on it, so a place where they feed is a natural reading
cafeteria.inference: the voles do eat the strip's seed, but more than half of those marked there are eaten by owls within a month, so the strip's role in their lives is where they die, not where they are fed

topic_tag: a coral outcrop in a lagoon
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Divers who have logged its visitors since 1985 call the outcrop the lagoon's ______.

worlds.passage: A lone coral outcrop the size of a car rises from the sand of a shallow lagoon, a quarter mile inside its ring of reef. By day, snappers and groupers from the outer reef gather near it in loose groups and take turns hanging head-down beside it, gill covers flared, while shrimp living in its crevices crawl over them and into their mouths. Each fish swims back to the reef within minutes of its turn. On a nearby reef where divers removed every shrimp, groupers now spend hours rubbing their flanks against the sand. Divers who have logged its visitors since 1985 call the outcrop the lagoon's ______.
worlds.explanation: "Clinic" fits: fish take turns hanging still while the outcrop's shrimp crawl over them and into their mouths, and where the shrimp were removed groupers rub themselves against the sand, which shows the shrimp had been ridding them of something that irritates them; the outcrop is where reef fish go to be cleaned. "Canteen" fails because the visitors hang motionless with mouths open while shrimp work on them; the visitors are being tended, not eating. "Bedroom" fails because the visits are by day and end within minutes. "Ballroom" fails because the groups are of mixed species, each fish hanging alone in its turn, with no courtship.

canteen.quote: hanging head-down beside it, gill covers flared
canteen.why: the visitors hold still while the shrimp work on them
canteen.surface_fit: fish swim in from the outer reef each day to a coral head, which is where reef fish usually feed, so a feeding stop is a natural reading
canteen.inference: fish that hang motionless with gills flared while shrimp crawl into their mouths, and that itch on reefs without the shrimp, come to have something removed, not to eat

bedroom.surface_fit: reef fish are known to shelter in coral heads, so an outcrop fish keep returning to sounds like a place to rest
bedroom.inference: a turn of a few minutes in daylight followed by a swim back to the reef is not rest; a sleeping place would hold the fish through the night

ballroom.why: mixed species waiting in turn, each alone, with no display
ballroom.surface_fit: groups of fish gathering at one coral head and waiting their turn sounds like the crowds reef fish form to court
ballroom.inference: snappers and groupers mixed together, each hanging alone in its turn, make no crowd of one species and no display between partners, which courtship needs

worlds.passage: A lone coral outcrop the size of a car rises from the sand of a shallow lagoon, a quarter mile inside its ring of reef. Every morning of the year, parrotfish from the outer reef arrive in loose schools and work their way along its flanks, beaks to the rock, past shrimp waving from its crevices, each staying an hour before swimming back. Corners divers fenced with mesh grow algae a foot long, while the rest of the outcrop stays cropped to a bare film, and by afternoon the schools are back on the reef. Divers who have logged its visitors since 1985 call the outcrop the lagoon's ______.
worlds.explanation: "Canteen" fits: parrotfish spend an hour each morning with their beaks to the rock, and algae grows long only where mesh keeps them off, so they come to the outcrop to eat its algae. "Clinic" fails because the fish keep moving along the rock working it with their beaks and swim past the shrimp; what the outcrop loses is algae, not anything removed from the fish. "Bedroom" fails because the schools come in the morning and are back on the reef by afternoon. "Ballroom" fails because the schools come every morning of the year and feed, with no seasonal gathering or courtship.

clinic.quote: beaks to the rock, past shrimp waving
clinic.why: the fish work the rock themselves and pass the shrimp by
clinic.surface_fit: reef fish visiting a lone coral head where shrimp wave from crevices is the classic picture of a cleaning station
clinic.inference: fish that keep moving with beaks to the rock, while algae grows a foot long only where they are fenced out, are taking algae from the outcrop, and they pass the shrimp rather than stopping to be tended

bedroom.quote: by afternoon the schools are back on the reef
bedroom.why: the fish use the outcrop only in the morning
bedroom.surface_fit: parrotfish are known to spend nights tucked into coral, so a sleeping place fits the topic
bedroom.inference: schools that arrive in the morning and are back on the reef by afternoon spend their nights elsewhere, so the outcrop is not where they sleep

ballroom.why: a daily routine, not a seasonal gathering
ballroom.surface_fit: schools of fish converging on one coral head sounds like the mass gatherings reef fish hold to court and spawn
ballroom.inference: schools that come every morning of the year, crop algae for an hour and leave form a feeding routine, while a courtship gathering is a brief, seasonal crowd

worlds.passage: A lone coral outcrop the size of a car rises from the sand of a shallow lagoon, a quarter mile inside its ring of reef. At dusk, parrotfish from the outer reef arrive by the hundred, and each wedges itself alone into a crevice, wraps itself in a film of mucus that keeps off biting parasites, and lies still until dawn. Then they swim back to the reef, where divers watch them graze all day, while algae on the bare rock between the outcrop's crevices grows a foot long. Divers who have logged its visitors since 1985 call the outcrop the lagoon's ______.
worlds.explanation: "Bedroom" fits: parrotfish arrive at dusk, tuck alone into crevices and lie still until dawn, then leave to feed on the reef, so the outcrop is where they spend the night. "Canteen" fails because the fish graze on the reef by day and leave the outcrop's algae to grow a foot long. "Clinic" fails because what protects them from parasites is the mucus each fish makes for itself; nothing on the outcrop treats them. "Ballroom" fails because, though they arrive by the hundred, each fish wedges itself alone into a crevice and lies still, with no display.

canteen.quote: where divers watch them graze all day
canteen.why: the fish feed on the reef and leave the outcrop's algae uneaten
canteen.surface_fit: parrotfish are grazers, and fish converging on a coral head suggests they come to eat there
canteen.inference: fish that graze on the reef all day while the algae between the outcrop's crevices grows a foot long are not feeding at the outcrop

clinic.quote: wraps itself in a film of mucus
clinic.why: the protection from parasites comes from the fish itself
clinic.surface_fit: the passage ties the visits to protection from parasites, and lone coral heads are known as cleaning stations
clinic.inference: the parasites are kept off by mucus each fish produces on its own body while it lies still, so the outcrop offers a place to lie, not any treatment

ballroom.quote: each wedges itself alone into a crevice
ballroom.why: solitary fish lying still, not a courting crowd
ballroom.surface_fit: hundreds of fish converging on one coral head at dusk sounds like the evening gatherings reef fish hold to court
ballroom.inference: fish that each go alone into a crevice and lie motionless until dawn are not displaying to partners, whatever their numbers

worlds.passage: A lone coral outcrop the size of a car rises from the sand of a shallow lagoon, a quarter mile inside its ring of reef. For a week after the first full moon of summer, groupers from reefs thirty miles away crowd around it by the thousand, males circling the larger females all afternoon. At dusk, pairs that have formed leave together for the outer reef's edge, where divers have filmed them spawning. Schools of the small fish groupers eat swirl among them all week, as large on the last day as on the first. Divers who have logged its visitors since 1985 call the outcrop the lagoon's ______.
worlds.explanation: "Ballroom" fits: thousands of groupers gather for a week after one full moon, the males circle the females through the afternoon, and pairs that form there leave together, so the outcrop is where they court and choose partners. "Bedroom" fails because the pairs leave at dusk and spawn at the outer reef's edge; the outcrop is where they pair off by day, not where they mate or spend the night. "Canteen" fails because the schools of small fish that groupers eat are as large at the end of the week as at the start, so the crowd of groupers is not feeding on them. "Clinic" fails because a crowd of thousands timed to one full moon a year, with males circling females, has gathered to court, not to have parasites removed.

bedroom.quote: leave together for the outer reef's edge
bedroom.why: mating happens elsewhere at night; the outcrop is the daytime courting ground
bedroom.surface_fit: fish that stay for days and form pairs there suggests a place where they rest or mate
bedroom.inference: pairs that leave the outcrop at dusk and spawn at the outer reef's edge neither spend the night nor mate at the outcrop; what happens there is circling and pairing off

canteen.quote: as large on the last day as on the first
canteen.why: the groupers leave their prey alone
canteen.surface_fit: thousands of groupers crowding the outcrop amid schools of their prey looks like predators at a rich feeding ground
canteen.inference: if the schools of fish groupers eat are as large at the week's end as at its start, a crowd of thousands of groupers has not been eating them, so the groupers did not come to feed

clinic.quote: after the first full moon of summer
clinic.why: a moon-timed yearly crowd is a courtship event, not cleaning visits
clinic.surface_fit: groupers are well known to visit coral heads to be cleaned, so groupers traveling there from distant reefs sounds like a trip to a cleaning station
clinic.inference: cleaning visits happen any day, fish by fish, while a crowd of thousands timed to one full moon a year, with males circling females, has gathered to court

topic_tag: a dam and the river below it
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Twenty years of surveys show that the dam has ______ the river below it.

worlds.passage: In 1960 a dam was built across a mountain river, holding back a reservoir three hundred feet deep. Twenty years of surveys show that the dam has ______ the river below it. Its turbines draw water from near the reservoir's floor and pass it through at an even rate, day and night, and each May the snowmelt flood pours over the spillway and rolls the gravel bars below. The stretch below the dam, once thick with bass, now holds almost none; trout spawn instead on gravel bars lying as deep under water as before 1960, and the bass have retreated to reaches thirty miles downstream.
worlds.explanation: "Chilled" fits: the turbines release water from the bottom of a deep reservoir, and below the dam trout have replaced bass, which now live only thirty miles downstream, so the river below has turned cold. "Bled" fails because the gravel bars lie as deep under water as before 1960, so the river below carries as much water as ever; the bass left for another reason. "Churned" fails because the release is even day and night, and the only surge is the river's own snowmelt flood spilling over in May, not anything the turbines do. "Clogged" fails because that flood still rolls the gravel bars every year, so silt and plants cannot settle and choke the channel.

bled.quote: lying as deep under water as before 1960
bled.why: the bars are as deeply covered as before, so the river has lost no water
bled.surface_fit: the stretch below the dam has lost its summer bass, and dams commonly draw water off for farms and cities, so a dam draining its river is a natural reading
bled.inference: gravel bars that sit as deep under water as before the dam mean the river below carries as much water as it did, so the loss of the bass came from something other than lost water

churned.quote: at an even rate, day and night
churned.why: the turbine release is steady and the spring flood is the river's own

"Crated" fails because the bell still hangs in the tower of the church on its old site, so the building was never taken apart and shipped away. "Commandeered" fails because the council barred everyone from the building and ivy has grown over its doors, so the council took it out of use rather than taking it over for its own.

topic_tag: weather and a fleet of sailing ships
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

worlds.passage: In 1789 a fleet of eleven sailing ships left port carrying settlers along a coast of sandy bays and rocky headlands. In its third week at sea, the weather ______ several of the fleet's ships. Water was cut to a pint a man. On the tenth morning a land breeze carried all five into harbor, a week behind the others.
worlds.explanation: "Becalmed" fits: for nine days the five ships made no progress past the same headland while their galley smoke rose straight up, so there was no wind to move them. "Blinded" fails because the crews sighted the headland every noon, so they could see where they were. "Beached" fails because the crews swam alongside the hulls, so the ships were afloat in deep water, not on the sand. "Capsized" fails because the ships kept their galley fires burning and the crews swam beside them in calm water before all five sailed into harbor, so none had rolled over.

blinded.why: the crews could see the coast
blinded.surface_fit: ships stuck for days off a rocky headland suggests fog that kept them from knowing where to steer
blinded.inference: crews who sighted the same headland every noon could see the coast clearly, so poor visibility was not what held them; they could see they were not moving

beached.quote: their crews swam alongside the hulls
beached.why: the ships were afloat in water deep enough to swim in
beached.surface_fit: ships that stay at the same spot on a coast of sandy bays for nine days sound like ships run aground
beached.inference: crews swimming alongside the hulls means the ships floated in deep water, and a land breeze moved them on, so they were never on the sand

worlds.passage: In 1789 a fleet of eleven sailing ships left port carrying settlers along a coast of sandy bays and rocky headlands. In its third week at sea, the weather ______ several of the fleet's ships. For nine days their crews gathered driftwood around the hulls at low tide, until the spring tide lifted all four and they sailed on.

"Blinded" fails because the lookouts saw the surf an hour ahead, so the crews could see the coast coming; the gale, not poor sight, put them there.

In its third week at sea, the weather ______ several of the fleet's ships. A squall struck the fleet broadside in mid-channel while three ships carried full sail. Within a minute their masts lay flat on the water, and their crews spent the night clinging to barnacled keels until ships that had shortened sail in time, a mile off, picked them up at dawn, having watched the three lanterns dip into the sea.

"Beached" fails because this happened in mid-channel and the crews had to be picked up by other ships, so there was no shore near. "Becalmed" fails because the ships were struck while carrying full sail in a squall, so they had more wind than they could bear. "Blinded" fails because ships a mile off watched the three lanterns go down, so the crews could see.

topic_tag: a whale carcass on the deep seafloor
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: A biologist who has filmed it since 1988 calls the carcass the seafloor's ______.

worlds.passage: In 1987 a forty-ton whale died at sea and sank to the seafloor two miles down. A biologist who has filmed it since 1988 calls the carcass the seafloor's ______. Within days hundreds of sleeper sharks, hagfish and crabs had crowded onto it from miles around, and in four months they had stripped its flesh; bacteria finished the bones within a year. The same kinds of animals turn up at any bait lowered onto that seafloor, and they scattered once the flesh was gone.
worlds.explanation: "Banquet" fits: hundreds of scavengers crowded onto the carcass at once and ate it all within months, one huge feast that ended when the flesh was gone. "Cupboard" fails because nothing was kept back to draw on later; the crowd consumed all of it in four months. "Battery" fails because the bones were finished within a year, so the carcass gave up its energy in a burst rather than slowly over a long time. "Bridge" fails because the scavengers are the kinds of animals that turn up at any bait on that seafloor, so the carcass linked no populations that were apart.

cupboard.surface_fit: a whale carcass is a huge store of food lying on the seafloor, which is just what a cupboard holds
cupboard.inference: a store is kept and drawn on over time, but hundreds of scavengers stripped all the flesh within four months and then scattered, so nothing was kept for later

battery.inference: flesh gone in four months and bones finished within a year means the carcass's energy was spent in a burst, not released slowly over a long time

worlds.passage: In 1987 a forty-ton whale died at sea and sank to the seafloor two miles down. A biologist who has filmed it since 1988 calls the carcass the seafloor's ______. For six years the same few sleeper sharks, known by their scars, came back every few weeks, each tearing off a mouthful or two of the cold flesh and swimming off with it. Tags showed that they came from deep basins on opposite sides of the carcass, and that each shark went home to its own basin. By 1994 the bones were bare.
worlds.explanation: "Cupboard" fits: the same few sharks returned every few weeks for six years, each tearing off a mouthful and taking it away, so the carcass was a store of food they drew on bit by bit. "Banquet" fails because there was no crowd and no single feast; a few sharks took a mouthful or two at a time. "Battery" fails because the carcass's flesh was eaten as it was, torn off and carried away, which is a larder's role; nothing on it was converting stored energy into power. "Bridge" fails because sharks from each basin went home to their own basin, so no animal crossed from one side to the other by way of the carcass.

banquet.inference: a few sharks taking a mouthful or two every few weeks for six years are drawing down stored food slowly, not sharing one great meal

battery.surface_fit: a store of food drawn down slowly over six years sounds like a battery running down
battery.inference: the sharks tear off the flesh and carry it away to eat, mouthful by mouthful, which is food taken from a store, not energy released on site to power anything

worlds.passage: In 1987 a forty-ton whale died at sea and sank to the seafloor two miles down. A biologist who has filmed it since 1988 calls the carcass the seafloor's ______. "Cupboard" fails because the clams cannot eat the oil; its energy reaches them only after bacteria convert it, like a stored charge slowly discharged, not a stock of food eaten as it is. "Banquet" fails because the bones have supported the bacteria and clams for thirty years without running down, which is the opposite of a brief feast. "Bridge" fails because young clams settle among their parents, so the carcass keeps its community in place rather than passing animals on.

"Banquet" fails because the biologist's point is where the clams came from and where their young went, lineages crossing between distant springs, not a crowd feeding. topic_tag: small birds on an island flowering tree, netting experiment
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: In those three years, the birds ______ the tree.

worlds.passage: On one island a single species of small bird drinks at the flowers of a native tree and roosts in its crown. For three years an ecologist netted the birds off some branches and compared them with open ones. Under the nets the flowers dropped whole, unbitten by insects. Caterpillars chewed netted and open leaves alike while the birds fed head-down in the blossoms, and nearly every flower a bird had probed swelled into a hard green fruit that fell unopened beneath the tree, where the island's few seedlings come up. In those three years, the birds ______ the tree.
worlds.explanation: Flowers the birds could not reach dropped whole without setting fruit, while nearly every flower a bird had probed set fruit, so the birds "pollinated" the tree. "Patrolled" fails because the birds spent their visits head-down in the blossoms and caterpillars chewed netted and open leaves alike, so the birds kept no insects off. "Propagated" fails because the fruit falls unopened beneath the tree, where the seedlings come up, so the birds carry no seed anywhere. "Parasitized" fails because the nectar the birds drink is repaid: without them the tree sets no fruit at all.

patrolled.quote: Caterpillars chewed netted and open leaves alike while the birds fed head-down in the blossoms
patrolled.why: The birds were busy in the flowers, and keeping them off changed no leaf damage.
patrolled.surface_fit: Birds living in a tree's crown all year are the ones that pick its pests off, and the netted flowers fail, so guarding is a natural first reading.
patrolled.inference: The birds spend their visits with their heads in the blossoms, and leaves under the nets were chewed no more than open ones, so the birds' presence keeps no insect off the tree; the flowers failed for another reason.

propagated.inference: The birds affect only whether fruit forms; the hard fruit falls unopened and the seedlings rise under the parent, so the birds never move a seed.

parasitized.why: Probed flowers set fruit and unvisited ones did not, so the birds give the tree something it needs.
parasitized.surface_fit: The birds take the tree's nectar and roost in it, living off it the way a parasite lives off a host, so the word fits the sentence and the topic.
parasitized.inference: Without the birds every netted flower dropped fruitless, while the flowers they probed set fruit, so the nectar they drink buys the tree its fruit; a visitor the tree cannot fruit without is not a drain on it.

topic_tag: nesting falcons and a city square's pigeons
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

worlds.passage: When a pair of peregrine falcons began nesting on a cathedral spire in 1996, birdwatchers began counting the pigeons in the square below each winter and banding their chicks each spring. Over the following decade, the falcons ______ the flock. By 2006 the square's winter count had halved, and banders who checked every roost in the city found none of its banded birds anywhere else. Most bands they picked up under the falcons' ledge had been fitted the spring before, so the banded birds left in the square were mostly old ones, and those went on nesting on the spire's lowest ledges, a few yards below the falcons.
worlds.explanation: The square's count halved while none of its banded birds turned up at any other roost in the city, so the missing pigeons had died, not moved: the falcons "reduced" the flock. "Redistributed" fails because the banders searched every roost in the city and found no square bird elsewhere, so the flock did not move. "Rattled" fails because the survivors went on nesting a few yards below the falcons, which unsettled birds would not do. "Rejuvenated" fails because the falcons took mostly birds banded the spring before, leaving the flock older.

redistributed.inference: The count halved and the banders checked every roost in the city without finding a square bird elsewhere, so the missing birds had not settled anywhere else; they were gone.

rattled.inference: Birds unsettled by the falcons would not raise their young a few yards beneath the falcons' nest, so the survivors' behavior shows no fear; the falcons' effect was on how many there were.

rejuvenated.why: The falcons took mainly last spring's young, so the flock aged.
rejuvenated.surface_fit: Predators are often said to keep a flock young and healthy by taking the old and weak, so the word fits a story about falcons and pigeons.
rejuvenated.inference: Most bands under the falcons' ledge came from birds less than a year old, and the banded survivors were mostly old, so the falcons made the flock older, not younger.

worlds.passage: When a pair of peregrine falcons began nesting on a cathedral spire in 1996, birdwatchers began counting the pigeons in the square below each winter and banding their chicks each spring. Most bands picked up under the falcons' ledge came from birds over five years old or crippled by the string that tangles city pigeons' feet, and with fewer mouths at the crumbs, far more chicks lived to a second spring, so by 2006 the winter count stood where it had in 1996.
worlds.explanation: The falcons took mostly old birds and birds crippled by string, and with fewer mouths at the crumbs more young survived, refilling the flock to its old count, so the falcons "rejuvenated" the flock, replacing old and lame birds with young ones. "Reduced" fails because the surviving young brought the count back to its 1996 level. "Redistributed" fails because the pairs kept to their old ledges. "Rattled" fails because the lowest pairs nested a few yards below the falcons, which unsettled birds would not do.

reduced.quote: the winter count stood where it had in 1996
reduced.why: The extra surviving chicks made up for the falcons' kills.
reduced.surface_fit: The falcons kill pigeon after pigeon, so a reader expects the flock to be smaller.
reduced.inference: The losses fell on old and lame birds, and the food they left let more chicks survive, so by 2006 the count had returned to its old level; the flock was changed in makeup, not shrunk.

redistributed.why: The pairs kept their old nest sites.
redistributed.surface_fit: Pigeons are expected to abandon a square overlooked by a falcon nest, so a shift in where the flock lives is the reader's first expectation.
redistributed.inference: The pairs raised their young on the same ledges as before, even the ones nearest the falcons, so the flock's place in the city did not change.

rattled.quote: the lowest a few yards below the falcons
rattled.why: Pigeons nested right under the falcons, so they were not made nervous.
rattled.surface_fit: Returning predators are commonly said to make prey jumpy, so rattled fits the sentence and the topic.
rattled.inference: Pairs that nest a few yards below a falcon nest are not unsettled by it, so the falcons did not change the flock's nerves; their effect was on which birds lived.

topic_tag: a poet's first collection, 1851
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Within two years, her poems had been ______.

worlds.passage: In 1851 a young poet paid a printer in her city to issue three hundred copies of her first collection, on terms that gave her a share of every copy sold. Within months, cheaper copies bearing her name and matching hers down to a misprint on page twelve were selling at half her price in her shops. Her printer had set no second edition, her quarterly share, paid only on his copies, fell that spring to almost nothing, and the shops sold barely more copies in all than before of a book the papers had named among the season's best. Within two years, her poems had been ______.
worlds.explanation: The cheap copies reproduced her edition down to its misprint, yet her printer had set no second edition, and her share, paid only on his copies, collapsed as the cheap ones sold; someone else was printing her book and paying her nothing, so her poems had been "pirated". "Plagiarized" fails because the copies bore her name, so no one claimed the poems as his own. "Popularized" fails because the shops sold barely more copies in all than before: the cheap copies took her buyers instead of finding new readers. "Panned" fails because the papers had named the book among the season's best.

plagiarized.why: The copies credited her, so the theft was of her income, not her authorship.
plagiarized.surface_fit: Someone other than her printer was selling her poems as their own product and taking the money, which a reader readily files under plagiarism.
plagiarized.inference: Plagiarism passes another's work off as one's own; these copies carried her name, so readers knew whose poems they were, and what was taken was the money from each sale.

popularized.quote: sold barely more copies in all than before
popularized.why: Total sales barely rose, so the poems reached hardly any new readers.
popularized.surface_fit: Copies at half price filling the shops sounds like the poems being spread to a wider public, so popularized is tempting.
popularized.inference: Her own copies stopped selling as the cheap ones sold, and the total barely rose, so the cheap copies replaced her sales to the same buyers rather than carrying the poems to new ones.

panned.surface_fit: Her sales collapsing within months is what happens to a first collection that critics savage, so panned fits the story.
panned.inference: The city papers ranked the book among the season's best, so her sales fell because cheaper copies undercut hers, not because critics attacked the poems.

worlds.passage: In 1851 a young poet paid a printer in her city to issue three hundred copies of her first collection, on terms that gave her a share of every copy sold. Within months a well-known poet published a collection whose longest poems followed hers image by image and stanza by stanza, every line reworded, under his name alone. The city papers had already named two of hers among the season's best, and her printer sold out her three hundred copies and printed no more, while his book sold about as many. Within two years, her poems had been ______.
worlds.explanation: A well-known poet published poems that followed hers image by image and stanza by stanza, reworded and signed with his name alone, so her poems had been "plagiarized": their substance was passed off as his. "Pirated" fails because he did not reproduce her text; every line was reworded and set in his own collection, so no copy of her poems was printed and sold. "Panned" fails because the city papers had named two of her poems among the season's best. "Popularized" fails because her printer stopped at three hundred copies and his book sold about as many, so neither version carried the poems to a wide public.

pirated.why: No line of her text was reproduced, so no unauthorized copy of her poems was printed.
pirated.surface_fit: Another writer took her poems and profited from them in print, which is close to what piracy of a book means, so the word fits the topic and the blank.
pirated.inference: Piracy is printing and selling copies of someone's work without leave; here the borrowed poems were rewritten line by line and issued as his own book, so what was taken was her invention and credit, not her printed text.

panned.quote: named two of hers among the season's best
panned.surface_fit: A first collection whose ideas are lifted by a famous rival and whose printer prints no more could easily be one that critics dismissed, so the word fits the story's air of failure.
panned.inference: The city papers ranked two of her poems among the year's best, so her poems were admired by critics; what went wrong is that another poet signed their images.

popularized.quote: printed no more, while his book sold about as many
popularized.why: Neither her edition nor his reached more than a few hundred readers.
popularized.surface_fit: A well-known poet putting her images into his own book might carry them to his larger audience, so a reader may see the poems spreading.
popularized.inference: Her printer stopped at three hundred and his collection sold about three hundred, so whichever name was on them, the poems reached only a few hundred readers, not a wide public.

worlds.passage: In 1851 a young poet paid a printer in her city to issue three hundred copies of her first collection, on terms that gave her a share of every copy sold. Within months a celebrated actress began reciting the poems, naming the poet each night, in sold-out halls across the country, and cheap editions appeared in every city she played. Each carried her printer's license on its back page, her share of every copy reached her within the quarter, and the city papers had already named two of the poems among the season's best. Within two years, her poems had been ______.
worlds.explanation: A celebrated actress recited the poems in sold-out halls across the country and cheap editions followed her from city to city, so her poems had been "popularized": carried to a wide public. "Pirated" fails because each cheap edition carried her printer's license and paid her share of every copy, so none was printed without leave. "Plagiarized" fails because the actress named the poet each night. "Panned" fails because the city papers had named two of the poems among the season's best.

pirated.quote: carried her printer's license on its back page
pirated.why: The cheap editions were licensed and paid her share.
pirated.surface_fit: Cheap editions springing up in city after city behind a touring performer is exactly how unauthorized printings of a popular book appeared in that era, so pirated is a strong first reading.
pirated.inference: Each cheap edition bore her printer's license and her share of every copy reached her, so the editions were printed with permission and paid for; copies made with leave and royalties are not pirated.

plagiarized.why: The actress credited the poet at every recital.
plagiarized.surface_fit: A famous performer presenting another's poems on her own stage is a common way credit gets taken, so a reader may suspect the actress claimed them.
plagiarized.inference: The actress named the poet at each recital, so audiences knew whose poems they were hearing; the work spread with its author's name on it.

panned.quote: named two of the poems among the season's best
panned.surface_fit: Poems that sweep the halls and cheap editions are often the kind critics sneer at as popular verse, so the word fits the topic.
panned.inference: The papers ranked two of the poems among the season's best, so the critics admired them rather than attacking them.

worlds.passage: In 1851 a young poet paid a printer in her city to issue three hundred copies of her first collection, on terms that gave her a share of every copy sold. Within months every city paper had reviewed the collection by printing her weakest stanza in full, under her name, beside a cartoon of a weeping cow, and her line comparing her heart to a farm cart was being recited at dinner parties to roars of laughter. A comic weekly ran verses of its own in her meter and on her subjects, signed by its editor, and her printer sold forty copies. Within two years, her poems had been ______.
worlds.explanation: The papers answered the book by reprinting its weakest stanza beside a cartoon of a weeping cow, her lines became a dinner-party joke, and the printer sold only forty copies, so her poems had been "panned": held up to ridicule by the critics. "Pirated" fails because the papers printed single stanzas inside reviews, and no one issued copies of the book to sell. "Plagiarized" fails because the comic weekly's verses were its own, signed by its editor, imitating her meter and subjects to mock her, not her lines passed off as his. "Popularized" fails because the lines were famous only as a joke: the book itself sold forty copies.

pirated.quote: printing her weakest stanza in full
pirated.why: Single stanzas quoted inside reviews are not copies of the book put on sale.
pirated.surface_fit: Her verse was being printed by every paper in the city without any sign of her leave, which looks like her work being reproduced by others.
pirated.inference: Each paper printed one stanza as the target of its review, and the only copies of the book were her printer's forty sold, so no one was selling her collection in an edition of their own.

plagiarized.quote: ran verses of its own in her meter and on her subjects
plagiarized.why: The weekly wrote its own verses imitating hers, so it took her manner to mock it, not her lines.
plagiarized.surface_fit: Another publication printing verses in her meter and on her subjects under its editor's name is just how plagiarism looks at first sight.
plagiarized.inference: The weekly's verses were its own words, written in her style while her own lines were circulating as a joke, so the imitation was mockery of her work, not her work claimed by someone else.

popularized.why: The book sold almost nothing, so the attention made the poems a joke, not a popular book.
popularized.surface_fit: Her lines were being recited at dinner parties all over the city, which sounds like the poems becoming widely known.
popularized.inference: People repeated her lines to laugh at them, and only forty copies sold, so the poems spread as ridicule without winning readers.

topic_tag: an occupying army and a port city's museum, 1797
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Within a year, the army had ______ the museum's collection.

worlds.passage: In 1797 an occupying army entered a port city whose museum held some four hundred paintings and bronzes, many of them carried off from neighboring towns by the city's own fleet a century earlier. By the army's first morning, the museum's cases stood open, their coins, cameos and small bronzes gone, and several canvases had been cut from their frames. When the council offered the commander a sum for their return, he answered that he knew nothing of them; pieces later surfaced one by one in pawnshops across the army's home country, pledged by men discharged from its ranks. Within a year, the army had ______ the museum's collection.
worlds.explanation: Overnight the cases were emptied of whatever could be carried and canvases were cut from their frames, the commander knew nothing of it, and the pieces later turned up pawned one by one by former soldiers, so the army's men had "ransacked" the collection, plundering it for themselves. "Ransomed" fails because when the council offered to pay for the pieces, no one on the army's side held them to sell back. "Requisitioned" fails because a requisition is an official taking for the army's use, and here the commander disowned the loss and the pieces were pawned by individual soldiers. "Repatriated" fails because the pieces went to pawnshops in the army's home country, not to the towns they had been taken from.

ransomed.quote: he answered that he knew nothing of them
ransomed.why: Payment was offered and no one was holding the pieces to sell back.
ransomed.surface_fit: An occupying army's commander being offered money for a city's missing treasures is the setup of a ransom, so the word fits the sentence and the story.
ransomed.inference: The council offered to pay, and the commander, who would have been the one holding them for a price, disclaimed all knowledge, while the pieces drifted into pawnshops one by one; nothing was being held for a sum.

requisitioned.quote: pledged by men discharged from its ranks
requisitioned.why: The pieces were turned into cash by individual soldiers, so they were not taken for the army's use.
requisitioned.surface_fit: An occupying army emptying a city's museum within a day of arriving is the classic setting for a military requisition, so the word is a natural first reading.
requisitioned.inference: A requisition is ordered by officers for the army's needs; here the commander disowned the loss, and the pieces were later pawned by discharged soldiers for themselves, so the taking was private plunder, not an official seizure.

repatriated.quote: in pawnshops across the army's home country
repatriated.why: The pieces went to the occupiers' own country, not back to the towns they came from.
repatriated.surface_fit: The opening says much of the collection had been taken from neighboring towns, which makes sending pieces home a natural thing for the blank to report.
repatriated.inference: The pieces surfaced in pawnshops in the army's homeland, pawned by its former soldiers, so none went back to the neighboring towns or anywhere they had come from.

worlds.passage: In 1797 an occupying army entered a port city whose museum held some four hundred paintings and bronzes, many of them carried off from neighboring towns by the city's own fleet a century earlier. Its officers crated every painting and bronze, listed each against a number, and stacked the crates under guard in the harbor fort, and the commander sent the council a copy of the list with a sum written beneath the total. When the council's bankers delivered that sum the next spring, the crates went back to the museum with their seals unbroken. Within a year, the army had ______ the museum's collection.
worlds.explanation: The officers crated and listed every piece, held the crates under guard, and sent the council the list with a sum beneath the total; once the sum was paid, the crates went back to the museum unopened, so the army had "ransomed" the collection. "Ransacked" fails because the pieces were crated, numbered and returned with their seals unbroken, the opposite of being rifled and scattered. "Requisitioned" fails because the army never put the pieces to any use: the crates sat under guard and went back once the city paid. "Repatriated" fails because the crates went back to the museum, not to the neighboring towns the pieces had come from.

ransacked.why: The crates were handled with care and returned intact, so nothing was rifled.
ransacked.surface_fit: An occupying army emptying a museum in its first months is exactly how a ransacking is usually told, so the word fits the topic and the blank.
ransacked.inference: Every piece was crated and numbered, and the crates came back sealed and unopened, so the collection was handled as property to be held intact, not torn through for loot.

requisitioned.quote: the crates went back to the museum
requisitioned.why: The army held the collection and released it for payment rather than putting it to its own use.
requisitioned.surface_fit: Officers crating and numbering a city's property and sending its council a signed list is how an official military seizure looks, so requisitioning is the obvious first reading.
requisitioned.inference: The crates sat unopened in the fort and were handed back once the bankers paid, so the army used the collection only as something to sell back; it never took the pieces for any use of its own.

repatriated.why: The pieces returned to the city's museum, not to the towns they had been taken from.
repatriated.surface_fit: The opening says many pieces had been carried off from neighboring towns, which makes returning them to those towns a natural thing for the blank to report.
repatriated.inference: The crates went back to the museum that held them before, so no piece was sent to any of the towns it had come from.

worlds.passage: In 1797 an occupying army entered a port city whose museum held some four hundred paintings and bronzes, many of them carried off from neighboring towns by the city's own fleet a century earlier. Its officers crated the bronzes and the largest canvases, listed each against a number, and left the council a copy signed by the commander. The bronzes went to the army's foundry and came out as cannon, the canvases were hung in the commander's headquarters, and the council's offer to buy them back was turned down. Within a year, the army had ______ the museum's collection.
worlds.explanation: The officers took the bronzes and big canvases under a signed list, melted the bronzes into cannon, hung the canvases in the commander's headquarters, and refused to sell them back, so the army had "requisitioned" the collection: seized it officially for its own use. "Ransacked" fails because the pieces were crated, numbered and signed for, not rifled. "Ransomed" fails because the council offered to buy the pieces back and the army refused. "Repatriated" fails because the pieces went to the army's foundry and headquarters, not to the towns they had come from.

ransacked.why: The taking was orderly and recorded, with a copy signed by the commander.
ransacked.surface_fit: An occupying army melting a city's bronzes and carrying off its paintings is destructive enough to read as ransacking, so the word fits the topic and the blank.
ransacked.inference: A ransacking is a disorderly hunt for loot; here officers crated chosen pieces, numbered them and gave the council a signed list, so the taking was methodical and on the record.

ransomed.quote: offer to buy them back was turned down
ransomed.why: The army refused payment, so it was not holding the pieces for a price.
ransomed.surface_fit: An army that takes a city's treasures and gives its council an exact list might well be preparing to sell them back, so ransom fits the sentence and the setting.
ransomed.inference: When the council offered to pay for the pieces, the army said no, because it was using them as cannon and decoration; holding something for payment and refusing payment cannot both be true.

repatriated.quote: went to the army's foundry and came out as cannon
repatriated.why: The pieces went to the army's own uses, not to their towns of origin.
repatriated.surface_fit: The opening says many pieces had been carried off from neighboring towns, so sending them back to those towns is a plausible thing for the army to have done.
repatriated.inference: The bronzes were melted down and the canvases hung in the commander's headquarters, so the pieces went to the army, not back to any town they came from.

worlds.passage: In 1797 an occupying army entered a port city whose museum held some four hundred paintings and bronzes, many of them carried off from neighboring towns by the city's own fleet a century earlier. Soldiers emptied half the galleries in a single night, wrapping each canvas in a blanket and leaving its frame on the wall. Officers had marked beforehand each piece whose old label named a neighboring town, and the crates, listed by number, sailed within the week to the towns on those labels, whose councils signed for them; this city's council was asked for no payment. Within a year, the army had ______ the museum's collection.
worlds.explanation: The opening says many pieces had been carried off from neighboring towns a century earlier; the officers took exactly the pieces whose labels named such a town and shipped each crate to the town on its label, so the army had "repatriated" the collection, sending the pieces to the places they were taken from. "Ransacked" fails because the night's haste followed a list drawn up beforehand: only marked pieces went, each wrapped and numbered, and each was signed for at its destination. "Requisitioned" fails because the army kept nothing for its own use; every crate sailed to the town named on its label. "Ransomed" fails because the city's council was asked for no payment.

ransacked.quote: Officers had marked beforehand each piece
ransacked.why: The removal followed a list drawn up in advance, with each piece numbered and signed for, which is selection, not plunder.
ransacked.surface_fit: Soldiers emptying half the galleries in one night and leaving bare frames on the walls is exactly what a ransacked museum looks like, so the word is the natural first reading.
ransacked.inference: Only the pieces marked beforehand by their labels were taken, each crate was numbered, and each was signed for by the receiving town, so the hasty night was the carrying out of a plan, not a hunt for whatever was valuable.

requisitioned.quote: sailed within the week to the towns on those labels
requisitioned.why: The crates went to the towns, not to the army's use.
requisitioned.surface_fit: Officers marking a city's property, crating it and listing it by number looks like an official military seizure, so requisitioning fits the sentence and the setting.
requisitioned.inference: A requisition takes goods for the army's own needs; these crates sailed to the towns named on their labels and were signed for by those towns' councils, so the army took nothing for itself.

ransomed.surface_fit: An army that crates a city's treasures and holds an exact list could be setting a price for their return, so ransom fits the setting and the sentence.
ransomed.inference: Ransoming means demanding payment for something's return; the council was never asked to pay, and the crates went to other towns rather than back to the museum.

topic_tag: an ancient clay tablet listing barley
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Scholars now read the tablet as its owner's ______.

worlds.passage: A clay tablet dug from the ruins of an ancient river city lists barley in nine lines, each giving an amount, a word or two, and a number, and a seal has been rolled across its back. The words name the hamlets of one village, and the numbers, rising from 2 to 27, are days of the harvest month on which grain from each hamlet reached the city storehouse, whose keeper's seal the tablet bears. It lay under the floor of the village headman's house, in a jar with his other sealed tablets. Scholars now read the tablet as its owner's ______.
worlds.explanation: The tablet records grain from the village's hamlets arriving at the storehouse, sealed by the storehouse keeper, and it was kept in the village headman's own house among his sealed tablets, so it is the headman's "receipt": the receiver's sealed acknowledgment of what the village delivered. "Roadmap" fails because the numbers are days of one harvest month on which grain reached one storehouse, so the named hamlets are where the grain came from, not stages of a journey. "Payroll" fails because the barley flows in from the village to the storehouse, not out to workers as pay. "Recipe" fails because each amount is a dated delivery from a named hamlet, not a quantity of an ingredient.

roadmap.quote: are days of the harvest month on which grain from each hamlet reached the city storehouse
roadmap.why: The numbers are dates within one month and every line ends at the same storehouse, so the list records deliveries, not stages of a route.
roadmap.surface_fit: Each line names a place with a number beside it, which is how a list of stops and travel days reads, so roadmap is a natural first reading.
roadmap.inference: The numbers rise through a single month as calendar days, and every line's grain went to one storehouse, so the places are sources of deliveries; no line is a leg from one place to the next.

payroll.why: The barley went into the storehouse, so nothing was paid out to workers.
payroll.surface_fit: Barley was the ordinary wage in ancient cities, and the tablet lists amounts with an official's seal, which is what a pay record looks like.
payroll.inference: A payroll lists what an employer hands out; these lines record grain arriving at the storehouse from the village's hamlets, so the barley runs the wrong way for wages.

recipe.quote: The words name the hamlets of one village
recipe.why: The words are places, not ingredients.
recipe.surface_fit: Barley measured out line by line in exact amounts is how an ancient brewing or baking tablet reads at first glance, so a recipe fits the topic.
recipe.inference: Every amount belongs to a hamlet and a day, so the list follows where and when grain arrived; nothing on it is to be combined or prepared.

worlds.passage: A clay tablet dug from the ruins of an ancient river city lists barley in nine lines, each giving an amount, a word or two, and a number, and a seal has been rolled across its back. The words are men's names, two of them marked as boys, whose amounts are cut by a fixed share, and each number, never above thirty, is the days that man worked that month; the seal is the temple overseer's. The tablet lay in the temple storeroom with eleven others, one for each month of that year, all listing the same nine men. Scholars now read the tablet as its owner's ______.
worlds.explanation: The tablet gives each of nine named men barley scaled to the days he worked that month, cut for the two boys, under the temple overseer's seal, and eleven matching tablets cover the year's other months, so it is the temple's "payroll": its record of wages paid out. "Receipt" fails because the seal is the payer's own and the tablet stayed in the payer's storeroom, so it is not anyone's sealed acknowledgment of goods received. "Roadmap" fails because the numbers are days worked by named men, the same nine every month, not days of travel between places. "Recipe" fails because the amounts belong to people, cut for the boys, not to ingredients.

receipt.quote: the seal is the temple overseer's
receipt.why: The sealer is the one paying out, and the tablet stayed with him, so it is not an acknowledgment of receipt.
receipt.surface_fit: Each line records barley a named man received, under an official's seal, which is close to what a receipt for goods looks like.
receipt.inference: A receipt is sealed by whoever received the goods and kept by whoever handed them over; here the seal is the payer's own and the tablet sits in his storeroom beside one for every month, so it is the payer's running record.

roadmap.quote: is the days that man worked that month
roadmap.why: The numbers count days of work by named men, not days of travel.
roadmap.surface_fit: Each line pairs an amount of barley with a number of days, which is how provisions for the legs of a journey are listed, so roadmap is tempting.
roadmap.inference: The days belong to named men, never exceed a month, and recur for the same nine men on every monthly tablet, so they measure work done, not distance traveled.

recipe.quote: whose amounts are cut by a fixed share
recipe.why: The scaling follows the worker, so the amounts are wages, not proportions of a mixture.
recipe.surface_fit: Barley measured in amounts line after line, some scaled down by a fixed share, reads like a list of proportions for a brew.
recipe.inference: The fixed cut applies to the two names marked as boys, so the amounts follow who received them, not a batch size; nothing here is combined or cooked.

worlds.passage: A clay tablet dug from the ruins of an ancient river city lists barley in nine lines, each giving an amount, a word or two, and a number, and a seal has been rolled across its back. The words run barley from the river fields, dates from the southern groves, water, then barley again, sprouted, and then crushed, and the numbers are days, three beside the sprouting and one beside the crushing. A second column repeats every amount exactly doubled, the seal is the temple brewer's, and the tablet lay among the brewery's jars. Scholars now read the tablet as its owner's ______.
worlds.explanation: The lines move through ingredients and then through stages of the same barley, sprouted and then crushed, with days of waiting beside the stages, and a second column doubles every amount, all under the brewer's seal, so the tablet is the brewer's "recipe": quantities and steps for a brew in two batch sizes. "Roadmap" fails because the days sit beside stages of one batch of barley, so the places named are only where the ingredients come from, not stops on a route. "Receipt" fails because a column that restates every amount at exactly twice the size sets out quantities to use, not goods someone acknowledged receiving, and the seal is the brewer's own. "Payroll" fails because no line names a person.

roadmap.quote: then barley again, sprouted, and then crushed
roadmap.why: The days time stages of one batch of barley, so the place names are ingredient sources, not stops.
roadmap.surface_fit: The lines name places, river fields and southern groves, with numbers of days beside some lines, which is how a list of stages and travel days reads.
roadmap.inference: The same barley appears again sprouted and then crushed, with the days beside those stages, so the days measure a process applied to one grain; the fields and groves only say where the ingredients came from.

receipt.why: A column that doubles every quantity scales a plan, which a record of goods received would never do.
receipt.surface_fit: A sealed tablet listing barley, dates and water in measured amounts looks like a storehouse record of deliveries, so receipt is a natural first reading.
receipt.inference: Goods received arrive in whatever amounts came, while this column restates the whole list at exactly twice the size, and the seal is the brewer's own, so the tablet sets out quantities to use.

payroll.quote: dates from the southern groves, water
payroll.why: The lines name foodstuffs, not people.
payroll.surface_fit: Barley was the common wage and the seal is a temple official's, so a column of barley amounts under it looks like a temple pay list.
payroll.inference: Every line's word is an ingredient or a stage of the barley, so nothing on the tablet is owed to any person; the amounts are portions of a mixture.

worlds.passage: A clay tablet dug from the ruins of an ancient river city lists barley in nine lines, each giving an amount, a word or two, and a number, and a seal has been rolled across its back. The words name towns in order up the river toward the mountains, each number is the days from the town before, and the barley, loaves and jars of beer beside it are scaled exactly to that many days for twenty donkeys and their drivers; the seal is a caravan master's. It lay in an inn at the river's mouth, where caravans set out. Scholars now read the tablet as its owner's ______.
worlds.explanation: The lines name towns in order up the river with the days from one to the next, and the food beside each line is scaled to that leg's days for the caravan, under a caravan master's seal, found where caravans set out, so the tablet is the caravan master's "roadmap": the stages of his route and what each leg needs. "Receipt" fails because each amount is computed from the days a leg will take, which fixes it before the journey; grain actually handed over would not track the next leg's length so exactly.
