worlds.passage: In 1859 a merchant built a log store at a mountain gold camp, the only building there with a stove, an iron safe and a shelf of bottles, and his ledger survives. One historian of the camp called the store, in those years, the camp's ______. Beside each watch, pistol or fiddle left in the safe, the ledger enters a sum paid to its owner, most of it spent on flour and powder. The same things reappear months later, most marked as taken back for that sum and a tenth more, the rest priced on the shelf beside the whiskey bottles, in a stove room that had no chairs.
worlds.explanation: Miners left watches, pistols and fiddles in the safe and received sums of money against them, then took them back for the sum plus a tenth or saw them priced for sale, so the store was the camp's "pawnshop": a lender against pledged goods. "Repository" fails because the goods were not simply kept for their owners: money was paid out against them, and unredeemed ones were put up for sale. "Pharmacy" fails because the bottles on the shelf held whiskey. "Parlor" fails because the stove room had no chairs, so it was where business was done, not where the camp sat together.

repository.surface_fit: Miners leaving their valuables in the store's iron safe is exactly what depositing things for safekeeping looks like, so repository fits the sentence and the setting.
repository.inference: A repository keeps what people leave and gives it back; here each item had a sum paid out against it, came back only for that sum and a tenth more, and was put up for sale if not redeemed, so the items were pledges.

pharmacy.why: The bottles held liquor, not medicine.

pharmacy.inference: The bottles on the shelf were whiskey, and the ledger records sums lent and repaid, not doses, so the store supplied no medicine.

parlor.inference: With no chairs in the stove room, miners came to pledge, redeem and buy, not to sit; the warmth served the trade, so the room was no shared sitting room.

worlds.passage: In 1859 a merchant built a log store at a mountain gold camp, the only building there with a stove, an iron safe and a shelf of bottles, and his ledger survives. topic_tag: a logging road over thirty years

worlds.passage: A two-lane road laid across a valley floor in 1960 carried loaded logging trucks for thirty years, and surveyors checked it each fall against stakes along its shoulders. Each July its asphalt softened in the heat, and the trucks, keeping to the same wheel tracks on the narrow lanes, pressed it a little lower every summer, most on the long climb, where they crawled. By then rain stood for days after every storm in two long lines up the climb, while at the stop sign below it, where the trucks braked hard, the asphalt lay as flat as the day it was laid. By 1990, its surface had been ______.
worlds.explanation: Softened asphalt was pressed a little lower each summer under trucks that always used the same wheel tracks, and by 1990 rain pooled for days in two long lines up the climb, so the surface had been "rutted": worn into grooves along the wheel paths. "Rippled" fails because folds come from braking trucks shoving asphalt forward, and at the stop sign, where they braked hard, the asphalt lay flat. "Raised" fails because the asphalt was pressed lower, not lifted. "Ruptured" fails because the rain stood in the grooves for days without draining away, so the asphalt beneath it held unbroken.

rippled.inference: Folds across a road come from braking wheels shoving soft asphalt forward; at the stop sign, where the braking happened, the surface stayed flat, so the deformation is the two lines along the climb, not crests across the road.

raised.quote: the stakes on either side of that line read the height at which the road was laid
raised.why: The ground moved sideways, not upward.
raised.surface_fit: An earthquake moving the ground under a road is often pictured as heaving it up, and the road was surveyed for height every fall, so raised fits the setting.
raised.inference: The stripe shifted six feet sideways while the stakes on both sides stayed at the laid height, so the movement was horizontal and lifted nothing.

rippled.quote: stepped six feet sideways where it crossed a line of springs
rippled.why: The stripe jumped once at a single line, which is a break, not a series of waves.
rippled.surface_fit: Earthquakes send waves through the ground, and a road shaken by one could be left wavy, so rippled is tempting.
rippled.inference: A stripe that runs straight and then steps six feet sideways at one line has been cut and offset there; waves would bend it up and down in many places, not shift it once.

rutted.quote: spread across both lanes through a gap in the asphalt
rutted.why: The damage is one tear across both lanes, not grooves along the wheel tracks.
rutted.surface_fit: Thirty years of loaded logging trucks is the usual cause of grooves in a road's wheel paths, so rutted is a natural reading.
rutted.inference: The asphalt was torn open across both lanes along the line of springs, crosswise to the traffic, so the damage runs across the road; grooves from trucks would run along it in the wheel tracks.

topic_tag: ants and the aphids they tend
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Her report concludes that the ants had ______ the aphids.

worlds.passage: For three summers an entomologist watched garden ants tend aphids on a row of beans, lapping up the honeydew the aphids release. When a shoot began to wilt, its aphids were gone from it within a day, and at dusk workers could be seen carrying aphids in their jaws along the stems. Aphids marked with paint on wilting shoots turned up the next morning on the youngest leaves of the same plant, feeding and walking off as briskly as unmarked ones. Her report concludes that the ants had ______ the aphids. On a row the ants could not reach, aphids stayed on wilting shoots until they starved.
worlds.explanation: "Herded" fits: aphids vanished from failing shoots, workers carried aphids along the stems at dusk, and the marked aphids reappeared next morning feeding on the freshest leaves, while untended aphids starved where they were, so the ants were moving their stock from poor feeding ground to good. "Devoured" fails because the aphids the workers carried off turned up alive and feeding the next morning. "Garnered" fails because the carried aphids were not taken in and kept: they were set down on the youngest leaves of the same plant. "Drugged" fails because the moved aphids walked off as briskly as any others, so their stillness in the ants' jaws was not sedation; the ants controlled where they fed by carrying them.

devoured.quote: turned up the next morning on the youngest leaves
devoured.why: The aphids carried off were found alive and feeding.
devoured.surface_fit: Aphids vanishing from shoots overnight while workers carry them off in their jaws looks exactly like ants taking prey, so "devoured" is a strong pull.
devoured.inference: The aphids disappeared from wilting shoots and were seen in the ants' jaws, but the marked ones turned up the next morning feeding on young leaves, so the ones carried off were moved, not eaten.

garnered.quote: on the youngest leaves of the same plant
garnered.why: The carried aphids were set down on fresh leaves, not collected.
garnered.surface_fit: Workers hauling aphids along the stems at dusk, when ants retreat to the nest, reads like a colony gathering its stock in, so "garnered" is tempting.
garnered.inference: Gathering in would end with the aphids stored somewhere; the marked aphids carried at dusk were found next morning out on the youngest leaves of the very plant they came from, so the ants were placing them, not collecting them.

drugged.quote: walking off as briskly as unmarked ones
drugged.surface_fit: Aphids that let themselves be lifted and carried without struggling look sedated, and ants are known to subdue aphids chemically, so "drugged" fits.
drugged.inference: Sedated aphids would stay sluggish after being set down; the marked aphids walked off as briskly as unmarked ones, so their stillness came from being carried, and what the ants controlled was where they fed.

worlds.passage: For three summers an entomologist watched garden ants tend aphids on a row of beans, lapping up the honeydew the aphids release. Tended aphids crept from leaf to leaf at a third the pace of untended ones, and few grew the wings aphids need to leave a plant. On bean leaves the workers had crossed, clipped and carried indoors far from any ant, untended aphids slowed the same way within an hour. Her report concludes that the ants had ______ the aphids. Both rows' aphids multiplied all summer, the untended ones three times as fast, spreading to plants the tended aphids never reached.
worlds.explanation: "Drugged" fits: tended aphids grew few wings and crept slowly, and untended aphids slowed the same way on leaves the workers had crossed, clipped and carried indoors, far from any ant, so something the ants leave on the leaves was restraining the aphids chemically. "Herded" fails because the restraint did not need the ants at all: aphids slowed on clipped leaves with no ant present, so it was a substance working on them, not ants gathering or steering a group. "Devoured" fails because the tended aphids multiplied all summer; their row ended with fewer only because its slowed, wingless aphids never spread to new plants. "Garnered" fails because the aphids were never collected anywhere: they went on multiplying out on the plants.

herded.quote: far from any ant, untended aphids slowed the same way
herded.why: The slowing happened with no ant present.
herded.surface_fit: The tended aphids stay put on their plants while untended ones spread, which looks like ants keeping a flock together, the textbook picture of ants herding aphids.
herded.inference: Herding is something the herder does to the flock; aphids set on leaves clipped from the ants' row slowed with no ant anywhere near them, so the restraint came from a trace on the leaves, not from ants keeping or steering them.

devoured.quote: Both rows' aphids multiplied all summer
devoured.why: The tended aphids increased all season.
devoured.surface_fit: The untended row ends with three times as many aphids as the tended one, which looks like the ants thinning out their aphids by eating them, so "devoured" is a strong pull.
devoured.inference: Eaten aphids would decline, but the tended aphids multiplied all summer; the untended row pulled ahead because its aphids spread over plants the slowed, wingless tended aphids never reached, so the gap comes from spreading, not eating.

garnered.quote: spreading to plants the tended aphids never reached
garnered.why: The aphids stayed out on the plants, multiplying.
garnered.surface_fit: The ants keep their aphids from leaving the row, which reads like a colony amassing a supply for itself, so "garnered" fits.
garnered.inference: Garnering means collecting and storing; the tended aphids were never moved or gathered, they simply multiplied where they were on the plants, more slowly than aphids free to spread, so nothing was collected.

worlds.passage: For three summers an entomologist watched garden ants tend aphids on a row of beans, lapping up the honeydew the aphids release. The aphids stayed on whatever shoot they had settled on, wilting or not, and walked as quickly on leaves the workers had crossed as on clean ones. As the beans withered in autumn, workers carried the aphids' eggs down into the nest, and a nest dug up in midwinter held thousands of them heaped in its deepest chamber. Her report concludes that the ants had ______ the aphids. In spring the eggs hatched there, and the young aphids climbed out to the new bean shoots.
worlds.explanation: "Garnered" fits: at the end of the season the workers collected the aphids' eggs, kept them heaped underground through the winter, and the next year's aphids came out of that store, so the ants gathered the aphids in and laid them up like a harvest. "Herded" fails because all summer the ants never moved aphids even off wilting shoots, and in spring the young climbed out on their own; the only carrying was eggs going into storage, not animals being driven to pasture. "Devoured" fails because the eggs taken underground were not eaten: they hatched in spring and the young left alive. "Drugged" fails because aphids walked as fast on ant-crossed leaves as on clean ones.

herded.quote: stayed on whatever shoot they had settled on, wilting or not
herded.why: The ants did not move aphids during the season, and in spring the young left the nest by themselves.
herded.surface_fit: The ants bring the aphids underground for winter and the young turn up on fresh spring shoots, like livestock brought in and let out to pasture, so "herded" is tempting.
herded.inference: Herding means driving animals between feeding grounds; these ants never moved an aphid off a dying shoot all summer, and the spring young climbed out on their own, so the one thing the ants did was carry eggs in and keep them, which is storing, not herding.

devoured.quote: the young aphids climbed out to the new bean shoots
devoured.why: The eggs taken underground survived and hatched.
devoured.surface_fit: Ants hauling thousands of aphid eggs down into the nest as food runs short in autumn looks exactly like a colony provisioning itself, so "devoured" fits on a first read.
devoured.inference: Eggs that were eaten could not hatch; the heaped eggs were still there in midwinter and hatched in spring into aphids that left the nest alive, so they had been kept, not consumed.

drugged.quote: walked as quickly on leaves the workers had crossed as on clean ones
drugged.why: Ant contact did not slow the aphids.
drugged.surface_fit: The aphids stay put on their shoots all summer even when the shoots wilt, which can look like animals kept docile by something the ants do to them.
drugged.inference: A drugged aphid would slow after ant contact; these walked as fast on ant-crossed leaves as on clean ones, so their staying put was not the ants' doing, and the ants' real act came in autumn.

worlds.passage: For three summers an entomologist watched garden ants tend aphids on a row of beans, lapping up the honeydew the aphids release. The aphids stayed on whatever shoot they had settled on, wilting or not, and walked as quickly on leaves the workers had crossed as on clean ones. When the beans dried and the honeydew dwindled, the clusters on the ants' row shrank by half within a week, and empty aphid skins, slit open, lay on the leaves beneath them. Her report concludes that the ants had ______ the aphids. On a row the ants could not reach, aphids lasted until the first frost.
worlds.explanation: "Devoured" fits: once the honeydew ran low, the aphids on the ants' row disappeared by half in a week, leaving slit-open empty skins where they had been, while aphids the ants could not reach survived until frost, so the ants turned on the aphids and ate them. "Garnered" fails because the emptied skins lay on the leaves right where the clusters had been, so the aphids were consumed on the spot, not collected and stored. "Herded" fails because the ants never moved the aphids, not even off wilting shoots. "Drugged" fails because aphids walked as fast on ant-crossed leaves as on clean ones.

garnered.quote: empty aphid skins, slit open, lay on the leaves
garnered.why: The aphids were killed and emptied where they sat, not carried off to be kept.
garnered.surface_fit: At the season's end the aphids vanish from the ants' row while they survive elsewhere, which looks like the colony gathering in its stock before winter, so "garnered" is tempting.
garnered.inference: Gathered-in aphids would be gone from the leaves entirely; instead their slit, emptied skins were left on the leaves under the shrinking clusters, so they were eaten in place rather than collected and stored.

herded.quote: stayed on whatever shoot they had settled on, wilting or not
herded.why: The ants never moved the aphids between shoots.
herded.surface_fit: Ants tending aphids for honeydew is the classic picture of ants herding livestock, and the passage opens with exactly that relationship.
herded.inference: Herding means moving animals to food; these aphids stayed even on wilting shoots, so the ants never steered them, and what the ants did at the end was kill them.

drugged.quote: walked as quickly on leaves the workers had crossed as on clean ones
drugged.why: Ant contact did not slow the aphids.
drugged.surface_fit: The aphids sit still in their clusters while the ants work through them, which can read as prey kept sluggish by something the ants apply.
drugged.inference: A drugged aphid would slow after ant contact; these walked as fast on ant-crossed leaves as on clean ones, so the ants were not sedating them.

topic_tag: a merchant shipwreck after two centuries
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Two centuries on the seabed had ______ the ship, divers reported after surveying it.

worlds.passage: A wooden brig loaded with roofing slates sank in thirty feet of water off a sandy coast that storms strike every winter. Two centuries on the seabed had ______ the ship, divers reported after surveying it. The hull rests upright on a ridge of rock that the current keeps bare of sand, its rails and hatch frames rounded into lumps of living stone. Divers had to chisel through three inches of oyster shell and coral before striking wood, and the oak beneath rang hard under the chisel. Through the open hatches, schools of fish swim in and out of the hold, among the stacked slates.
worlds.explanation: "Encrusted" fits: the rails and hatch frames have been rounded into living stone, and the divers had to chisel through inches of shell and coral to reach the oak, so sea life has built a hard crust over the ship's surfaces. "Entombed" fails because the ship is not sealed away: it sits on rock the current keeps clear of sand, and fish swim freely through its open hatches, so the crust covers its outside without enclosing it. "Dismantled" fails because the hull rests upright with its rails, hatches and stacked cargo still in place, storms notwithstanding. "Gnawed" fails because the oak under the crust rang hard under the chisel; the life on the wreck grew over the wood rather than into it.

entombed.quote: schools of fish swim in and out of the hold
entombed.why: The hull is open to the sea, not sealed in.
entombed.surface_fit: A wreck on a sandy coast is usually swallowed by sand, and a ship wrapped in inches of living stone can look sealed inside it, so "entombed" is a strong pull.
entombed.inference: Entombing means enclosing and sealing away; this hull sits on rock the current keeps bare of sand, and fish pass freely through its open hatches into the hold, so the stone lies only on its surfaces and the ship itself is open sea.

dismantled.quote: rests upright on a ridge of rock
dismantled.why: The hull is whole and in place.
dismantled.surface_fit: Storms strike the coast every winter and the ship's outline has been blurred into lumps, so "dismantled" is tempting.
dismantled.inference: A dismantled ship would lie in separated pieces; this hull rests upright, its rails and hatch frames still there under the crust and its slates still stacked in the hold, so the storms have not taken it apart.

gnawed.quote: the oak beneath rang hard under the chisel
gnawed.why: The wood under the crust is sound.
gnawed.surface_fit: Timber left in the sea for two centuries is the classic food of boring creatures, and this wreck is thick with sea life, so "gnawed" fits.
gnawed.inference: Wood that creatures had bored into would come up soft; the divers' chisel went through the shell and rang on hard oak, so the creatures settled on the wood without eating it.

worlds.passage: A wooden brig loaded with roofing slates sank in thirty feet of water off a sandy coast that storms strike every winter. Two centuries on the seabed had ______ the ship, divers reported after surveying it. Within a few years a sandbar drifting along the coast came to rest over the place where it sank, and the divers found the hull only by probing down with steel rods. Shipworms riddle the driftwood on that beach, and a plank the divers lifted from eight feet down took a nail like new timber. Pumped clear, the deck still showed its builders' tool marks, and the slates lay stacked in the hold.
worlds.explanation: "Entombed" fits: soon after the wreck a sandbar settled over it, the divers could find the hull only by probing down eight feet, and beneath the sand the ship lay sealed and preserved, so the seabed buried it. "Gnawed" fails because, although shipworms riddle the wood on that beach, the sand shut the hull off from the water they live in, and its oak took a nail like new timber. "Encrusted" fails because a hull covered within a few years never stood in open water long enough for life to settle on it; its deck still showed the builders' tool marks. "Dismantled" fails because the storms that shift the sandbar left the hull together, its slates still stacked in the hold.

gnawed.quote: took a nail like new timber
gnawed.surface_fit: Shipworms riddle the driftwood on this very beach, so "gnawed" is the natural guess for a wreck two centuries old.
gnawed.inference: The worms are in the beach's exposed wood; this hull has lain under eight feet of sand since its first years, cut off from the water the worms live in, and a plank lifted from it took a nail like new, so the sand kept them out.

encrusted.quote: still showed its builders' tool marks
encrusted.why: The deck's surface is bare and unchanged.
encrusted.surface_fit: Old wrecks are usually coated in shells and coral, so "encrusted" is the stock description of a ship after two centuries underwater.
encrusted.inference: A crust forms only on surfaces open to seawater; a sandbar covered this hull within a few years, and its deck surface still shows the builders' tool marks, so nothing ever grew over it.

dismantled.quote: the slates lay stacked in the hold
dismantled.why: The hull and its cargo are intact.
dismantled.surface_fit: A drifting sandbar on a coast storms strike every winter suggests a ship pounded apart, so "dismantled" is tempting.
dismantled.inference: A ship broken apart would spill its heavy cargo; the slates still lay stacked in the hold under the deck, so the hull held together under the sand.

worlds.passage: A wooden brig loaded with roofing slates sank in thirty feet of water off a sandy coast that storms strike every winter. Two centuries on the seabed had ______ the ship, divers reported after surveying it. The hull lies where it settled on open sand that the current sweeps clean each tide, and its outline, keel to rails, can still be traced from above. A plank the divers lifted weighed less than a loaf and crumbled in their hands. Its surface was pale and smooth except for holes no wider than a pencil lead, and slates that slid through the sagging planks lie crusted with barnacles around the hull.
worlds.explanation: "Gnawed" fits: a plank that looks smooth outside, apart from pencil-lead holes, weighs almost nothing and crumbles, so creatures have eaten the wood away from within. "Entombed" fails because the current sweeps the sand off the hull every tide, leaving it exposed. "Encrusted" fails because the barnacles are on the spilled slates, while the plank's own surface came up pale and smooth. "Dismantled" fails because the hull's outline can still be traced from keel to rails; the planks are sagging where they are, eaten hollow, not broken apart and scattered.

entombed.quote: open sand that the current sweeps clean each tide
entombed.why: The hull is exposed, not buried.
entombed.surface_fit: The wreck lies off a sandy coast where sand buries most wrecks, so "entombed" fits the setting.
entombed.inference: Entombing would need sand closed over the hull; the current sweeps it clean every tide and the outline can be traced from above, so the hull lies open to the water, which is how the borers reached it.

encrusted.quote: Its surface was pale and smooth
encrusted.why: The plank itself carries no crust.
encrusted.surface_fit: Barnacles crust the slates lying around the hull, so "encrusted" seems to describe the wreck.
encrusted.inference: The barnacles are on the slates that slid out; the plank's own surface was pale and smooth apart from tiny holes, so the creatures that changed the wood worked inside it, not on it.

dismantled.quote: its outline, keel to rails, can still be traced
dismantled.why: The hull's shape is intact on the bottom.
dismantled.surface_fit: Planks that crumble in the hand and cargo spilling through a sagging hull suggest a ship falling to pieces, so "dismantled" is tempting.
dismantled.inference: A dismantled ship would lie in separated pieces; this hull's outline can still be traced from keel to rails where it settled, so its timbers are in place and hollowed, not pulled apart.

worlds.passage: A wooden brig loaded with roofing slates sank in thirty feet of water off a sandy coast that storms strike every winter. Two centuries on the seabed had ______ the ship, divers reported after surveying it. Its slates lie scattered over half a mile of sea floor in a line running the way the winter storms blow, and planks and ribs turn up all along that line, some half buried, some bare, rarely in the same place two winters running. The planks the divers lifted were heavy and sound, their edges rounded and scoured pale by moving sand.
worlds.explanation: "Dismantled" fits: the cargo lies strung along the storms' track and the ship's own planks and ribs turn up along that same line, so the winters have broken the hull apart and carried it off piece by piece. "Entombed" fails because the pieces that lie half buried one winter are elsewhere the next, so the sand covers them only for a time and never seals them away. "Encrusted" fails because pieces kept moving and scoured by sand came up pale, with nothing settled on them. "Gnawed" fails because the planks were heavy and sound.

entombed.quote: rarely in the same place two winters running
entombed.why: The pieces keep moving, so the sand never seals them in.
entombed.surface_fit: Some of the wreck lies half buried in the sand off this sandy coast, so "entombed" is a strong pull.
entombed.inference: Being half buried one winter means little if the piece lies somewhere else the next; these pieces are shifted by each winter's storms, so the sand never closes over the ship and holds it.

encrusted.surface_fit: Wreck timber two centuries underwater is usually coated in shells, so "encrusted" is the stock description.
encrusted.inference: Shells and coral need a still surface to settle on; planks that move every winter came up rounded and scoured pale by the sand, so nothing could crust on them.

gnawed.why: The wood has not been eaten away.
gnawed.surface_fit: Scattered, worn wreck timber two centuries old suggests wood eaten by boring creatures, so "gnawed" fits.
gnawed.inference: Wood eaten by borers comes up light and weak; these planks were heavy and sound, so the ship's damage lies in being broken apart, not in its wood being eaten.

topic_tag: an estate's brick orchard wall
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Estate letters of the next fifty years treat the wall as the orchard's ______.

worlds.passage: In 1760 a riverside landowner built a brick wall twelve feet high and a quarter mile long beside his orchard, near a village of thatched cottages. It runs along the orchard's northern edge, open at both ends, and the river runs past the orchard's southern edge, with the village on its far bank. Peaches trained on the wall's sunny face set fruit in springs when frost blackens every other blossom, and the bricks there stay warm to the hand at midnight. A fire in 1791 burned the village to the ground and never crossed the water. Estate letters of the next fifty years treat the wall as the orchard's ______.
worlds.explanation: "Hearth" fits: the bricks on the wall's sunny face hold heat into the night, and the peaches trained against them set fruit in springs when frost kills the blossom everywhere else, so the wall is the orchard's source of warmth. "Fence" fails because the wall runs along one edge only and is open at both ends, so it closes nothing in or out. "Dike" fails because the river runs past the orchard's southern edge while the wall stands on its northern edge, with the trees between them, so the wall cannot hold the river off the orchard. "Firebreak" fails because the village lies across the river, and when it burned, the fire stopped at the water; it never came near the wall on the orchard's far side.

fence.why: A wall on one edge, open at both ends, encloses nothing.
fence.surface_fit: A high brick wall built beside an orchard is most often there to keep animals and thieves out, so "fence" is the natural first guess.
fence.inference: A fence has to enclose or bar a boundary; this wall runs along only the northern edge and is open at both ends, so anything could walk round it into the orchard.

dike.quote: the river runs past the orchard's southern edge
dike.why: The orchard lies between the river and the wall.
dike.surface_fit: The estate is on a river, and a long, heavy brick wall beside low farmland is just what a flood wall looks like, so "dike" fits the setting.
dike.inference: A dike must stand between the water and the land it protects; the river runs past the southern edge and the wall stands on the northern edge, so river water would reach the trees before it ever reached the wall.

firebreak.why: The river, not the wall, kept the village fire from the orchard.
firebreak.surface_fit: The thatched village burned to the ground and the orchard survived, and a solid brick wall is a classic fire barrier, so "firebreak" is a strong pull.
firebreak.inference: The village stands on the river's far bank and the fire stopped at the water; the wall is on the orchard's northern edge, away from the river, so the fire never reached it and the wall played no part in saving the trees.

worlds.passage: In 1760 a riverside landowner built a brick wall twelve feet high and a quarter mile long beside his orchard, near a village of thatched cottages. It encloses the orchard, with one locked gate, and pears are trained against its sunny inner face. Deer strip young trees outside it each winter and leave the orchard's trees alone. The frost of 1797 took every blossom in the orchard. The orchard sits on the estate's highest ground, and in 1791 sparks from a burning cottage blew over the wall and set its grass alight. Estate letters of the next fifty years treat the wall as the orchard's ______.
worlds.explanation: "Fence" fits: the wall closes the orchard in on every side with one locked gate, and the deer that strip young trees outside it leave the orchard's trees alone, so it keeps animals out. "Hearth" fails because even the pears trained against its sunny face lost their blossom in the frost of 1797, so the wall's bricks gave the trees no protecting warmth. "Dike" fails because the orchard sits on the estate's highest ground, where floodwater cannot reach it, so the wall has no river to hold back. "Firebreak" fails because sparks from the burning cottage blew over the wall and set the orchard's grass alight, so the wall did not stop fire.

hearth.quote: took every blossom in the orchard
hearth.why: Even the wall-trained pears lost their blossom to frost.
hearth.surface_fit: Pears are trained flat against the wall's sunny face, exactly the way heat-storing fruit walls were used, so "hearth" is a strong pull.
hearth.inference: A wall that stored heat would save the blossom trained against it; the 1797 frost took every blossom in the orchard, wall pears included, so the bricks gave the trees no warmth that mattered.

dike.quote: sits on the estate's highest ground
dike.why: The orchard is above any flood.
dike.surface_fit: The estate is a riverside one, and a long, thick brick wall around low farmland looks like flood protection, so "dike" fits the setting.
dike.inference: A dike holds water off low land; this orchard sits on the estate's highest ground, so river floods never reach the wall, and it holds back nothing.

firebreak.quote: blew over the wall and set its grass alight
firebreak.why: Fire got into the orchard over the wall.
firebreak.surface_fit: A thatched village stands nearby and a cottage did burn, and a solid brick wall around an orchard looks like it would stop flames, so "firebreak" is tempting.
firebreak.inference: A firebreak stops a fire from spreading; when a cottage burned, its sparks crossed the wall and lit the orchard's grass, so the wall did not keep fire out.

worlds.passage: In 1760 a riverside landowner built a brick wall twelve feet high and a quarter mile long beside his orchard, near a village of thatched cottages. It runs along the riverbank on the orchard's south side, footed below the waterline. Each spring the river rises nearly to its top and floods the meadows upstream and down. The orchard's north side lies open to pasture rising to the village. When spring frost blackens the blossom, it blackens every tree, those beside the wall too. A fire in 1791 burned the village and died out in the pasture. Estate letters of the next fifty years treat the wall as the orchard's ______.
worlds.explanation: "Dike" fits: the wall stands on the riverbank footed below the waterline, and each spring the river rises nearly to its top and floods the meadows on either side, so the wall is what holds the river off the orchard. "Hearth" fails because frost blackens the blossom on the trees beside the wall as much as on any other, so the wall gives no warmth. "Fence" fails because the orchard's north side lies open to the pasture, so the wall closes off only the river side. "Firebreak" fails because the village fire died out in the pasture on the orchard's open north side; the wall stands on the far, river side and never met it.

hearth.why: Trees beside the wall lose their blossom to frost like the rest.
hearth.surface_fit: Brick orchard walls are known for storing the sun's heat for fruit trees, so "hearth" fits the topic of an orchard wall.
hearth.inference: A wall that stored heat would spare the blossom growing beside it; frost blackens the trees beside this wall along with every other tree, so the wall warms nothing.

fence.quote: north side lies open to pasture
fence.why: The orchard is open on the far side.
fence.surface_fit: A long, high wall along an orchard's edge is the usual way to keep livestock and thieves out, so "fence" is a natural guess.
fence.inference: A fence must close the ground it guards; the orchard's north side lies open to the pasture, so animals could walk in freely and the wall bars only the river side.

firebreak.why: The fire stopped in the pasture, on the side without a wall.
firebreak.surface_fit: The thatched village burned to the ground while the orchard survived, and a solid brick wall is a classic fire barrier, so "firebreak" is a strong pull.
firebreak.inference: The village is up the pasture on the orchard's open north side, and the fire died out in that pasture; the wall stands on the south side along the river, so the fire never reached it and the wall did nothing to stop it.

worlds.passage: In 1760 a riverside landowner built a brick wall twelve feet high and a quarter mile long beside his orchard, near a village of thatched cottages. It runs along the orchard's northern edge, between trees and cottages, open at both ends, and village cattle wander round its ends to graze among the trees. The orchard slopes down from the wall to the river. The frost of 1797 took all the blossom, the rows nearest the wall as well. In 1791 fire burned every cottage, and the orchard lost only the scorched leaves of one row. Estate letters of the next fifty years treat the wall as the orchard's ______.

furrowed.inference: Furrows would be lines worn into the slope; the tracks are on the cattle's ridge, and this flock wanders as it crops, leaving its own slope unmarked.

fertilized.why: The droppings do not enrich the turf.
fertilized.surface_fit: A flock grazing one slope for two centuries suggests ground enriched by dung, and the grazed slope blooms with flowers the other lacks, so "fertilized" is tempting.
fertilized.inference: Enriched turf would grow greener around the droppings; it grows no greener, so the flowers come from the short cropping that lets them reach the light, not from richer ground.

topic_tag: an engraved copy of a coastal survey
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Setting the two side by side, a historian found that the engraver had ______ the survey.

worlds.passage: In 1590 a printer issued an engraved chart of a stretch of coast, copied from a navy surveyor's hand-drawn map. Laid over the survey on a light table, the print matches it line for line along forty miles of coast, compass rose and scale bar included, until the navy's own harbor. There the print's channel runs half a mile east of the surveyor's soundings, over water his notes mark as rock, and two shoals found nowhere in his notes lie across the channel he sounded. Foreign captains bought the print by the hundred. Setting the two side by side, a historian found that the engraver had ______ the survey.
worlds.explanation: "Doctored" fits: the print reproduces the survey exactly except at the navy's own harbor, where its channel runs over rock and invented shoals block the real one, on a chart sold in quantity to foreign captains, so the engraver falsified the survey at the one place where misleading other navies mattered. "Flipped" fails because the print lies over the survey line for line, compass rose included, so nothing is reversed. "Enlarged" fails because a print that matches the survey line for line on a light table is drawn at the survey's own size. "Gilded" fails because the only things the print adds are two shoals across a real channel, which change the chart's facts rather than dress it up.

flipped.quote: compass rose and scale bar included
flipped.why: The print lies over the survey in its own orientation.
flipped.surface_fit: The harbor's channel appears in the wrong place on the print, and engraved copies of the period were often reversed, so "flipped" is tempting.
flipped.inference: A reversed print could not lie over the survey line for line with even its compass rose in register; this one does along forty miles, so the change at the harbor is local, not a reversal.

enlarged.quote: matches it line for line along forty miles of coast
enlarged.why: The print overlays the survey exactly, so it is the same size.
enlarged.surface_fit: Printed charts were often redrawn at a new scale, and the print's channel lies half a mile from where the survey puts it, which looks like a change of scale, so "enlarged" fits.
enlarged.inference: An enlarged copy could not lie line for line over the original; this print does, for forty miles, so the half-mile shift at the harbor is a moved channel, not a bigger drawing.

gilded.quote: two shoals found nowhere in his notes
gilded.why: The additions are false hazards, not ornament.
gilded.surface_fit: The engraver plainly added things to the print that the survey lacks, and printed charts were often dressed up for buyers, so "gilded" fits.
gilded.inference: Gilding adds ornament that leaves the substance unchanged; the print's additions are shoals placed across the real channel and a channel moved onto rock, so they change what a captain would steer by.

worlds.passage: In 1590 a printer issued an engraved chart of a stretch of coast, copied from a navy surveyor's hand-drawn map. Laid over the survey on a light table, the print matches almost nothing. Turned face down and held against a window, it matches the survey line for line, every cape and shoal at its surveyed spacing, its lettering then reading backward. Two captains who steered by the print ran aground in its first year. Setting the two side by side, a historian found that the engraver had ______ the survey.
worlds.explanation: "Flipped" fits: the print fails to match the survey face up but matches it line for line when turned over and seen through the paper, so it is the survey's mirror image. "Doctored" fails because, once reversed, every cape and shoal sits at exactly its surveyed spacing; nothing was moved or invented, and the groundings came from reading a mirror image. "Enlarged" fails because the reversed print matches the survey line for line, so it is the same size. "Gilded" fails because seen that way it matches line for line, so the engraver added nothing to it.

doctored.quote: every cape and shoal at its surveyed spacing
doctored.why: Reversed, the print matches the survey exactly.
doctored.surface_fit: The print does not match the survey and captains who trusted it ran aground, which looks like a deliberately falsified navy chart, so "doctored" is a strong pull.
doctored.inference: A doctored chart would misplace chosen features; turned over, this print puts every cape and shoal at its surveyed spacing, so the whole survey is there unaltered and the mismatch comes from its being reversed.

enlarged.quote: it matches the survey line for line
enlarged.why: The print is the survey's size.
enlarged.surface_fit: The print does not match the survey when laid over it, and engravers often redrew charts at a new scale, so "enlarged" fits.
enlarged.inference: An enlarged copy could not match line for line in any position; turned face down this print does, so it is the survey's size and only its orientation differs.

gilded.quote: held against a window, it matches
gilded.why: Nothing was added to the print.
gilded.surface_fit: Engravers commonly dressed printed charts up for buyers, so "gilded" fits the topic.
gilded.inference: Ornament would show up as extra lines when the print is held over the survey; seen through the paper it matches line for line, so the engraver added nothing.

worlds.passage: In 1590 a printer issued an engraved chart of a stretch of coast, copied from a navy surveyor's hand-drawn map. Laid over the survey on a light table, the print matches it nowhere, its coast running off the survey's edges. Walked headland by headland from west to east with dividers, every gap on the print proves exactly double the same gap on the survey, and the print's scale bar, also doubled, turns each back into the distance the surveyor sounded. Its margins hold only coast and soundings. Setting the two side by side, a historian found that the engraver had ______ the survey.
worlds.explanation: "Enlarged" fits: the print's coast runs past the survey's edges, every gap between headlands is exactly double, and a doubled scale bar converts each back to the surveyed distance, so the engraver copied the survey at twice its size. "Doctored" fails because the doubled scale bar returns every distance to what the surveyor sounded, so no fact was falsified. "Flipped" fails because the headlands run in the same west-to-east order as on the survey. "Gilded" fails because the print's margins hold only coast and soundings, with nothing added for show.

doctored.quote: turns each back into the distance the surveyor sounded
doctored.why: Every distance reads true on the print's own scale.
doctored.surface_fit: The print matches the survey nowhere when laid over it, which looks like an engraver altering a navy chart, so "doctored" is a strong pull.
doctored.inference: A doctored chart misstates distances; every gap on this print is exactly double and its scale bar is doubled too, so a captain measuring with it gets the survey's true coast.

flipped.quote: headland by headland from west to east
flipped.why: The headlands run in the survey's order.
flipped.surface_fit: The print fails to match the survey on the light table, and engraved copies were often reversed, so "flipped" is tempting.
flipped.inference: A flipped print would run east to west; walked west to east, its headlands come in the survey's own order, each gap double, so the mismatch is one of size, not direction.

gilded.quote: Its margins hold only coast and soundings
gilded.surface_fit: A print larger than its original sounds like a showpiece made for display, so "gilded" fits.
gilded.inference: Gilding would add ornament; the print's margins hold only coast and soundings, so the larger sheet carries nothing but the survey drawn bigger.

worlds.passage: In 1590 a printer issued an engraved chart of a stretch of coast, copied from a navy surveyor's hand-drawn map. Laid over the survey on a light table, the print matches it line for line along the coast. Out in the open water, which the surveyor left blank, the engraver set spouting whales, a galleon under full sail, and a sea god blowing a conch, and around the plain title he cut a scrolled frame of fruit and cherubs. Merchants hung the print in their counting houses. Setting the two side by side, a historian found that the engraver had ______ the survey.
worlds.explanation: "Gilded" fits: the coast matches the survey exactly, and everything new on the print is ornament in empty water or around the title, so the engraver dressed up the survey without changing it. "Doctored" fails because the additions sit in water the surveyor left blank, while the coast itself matches line for line, so nothing a captain steers by is false. "Flipped" fails because the print lies over the survey line for line, in its own orientation. "Enlarged" fails because a print that overlays the survey line for line is drawn at its size.

doctored.why: The additions are in empty water, off the coast.
doctored.surface_fit: The engraver added many things to a navy chart that the surveyor never drew, which is how charts were falsified, so "doctored" is tempting.
doctored.inference: Falsifying a chart means changing what it records; the whales, ship and sea god sit in water the surveyor left blank, and the coast matches line for line, so the record itself is untouched.

flipped.quote: the print matches it line for line
flipped.why: The print lies over the survey in its own orientation.
flipped.surface_fit: Engraved copies of the period were often reversed in printing, so "flipped" is a plausible change.
flipped.inference: A reversed print could not lie line for line over the survey face up; this one does along the whole coast, so nothing was reversed.

enlarged.quote: line for line along the coast
enlarged.why: The print overlays the survey, so it is the same size.
enlarged.surface_fit: A print crowded with a galleon, whales and a framed title sounds like a grand showpiece, larger than a working survey, so "enlarged" fits.
enlarged.inference: An enlarged copy could not be laid over the original and match; this one matches line for line, so the ornaments were fitted onto a sheet of the survey's size.

topic_tag: beavers in a dry mountain valley
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: A hydrologist who has studied both valleys concludes that the beavers have ______ theirs.

worlds.passage: For thirty years beavers have lived on a creek in a dry mountain valley; the creek in the next valley has none. Where a hay meadow once lay, ducks now dive, and a line of gray pine trunks, barkless and bare of needles, stands out in open water. The beavers build with willow cut along the banks, which sprouts again from the stumps each spring, and silt settling behind each dam has raised the pond floors a foot. A hydrologist who has studied both valleys concludes that the beavers have ______ theirs. Beyond the water's edge, the valley's grass browns by midsummer just as the next valley's does.
worlds.explanation: "Flooded" fits: ducks dive where a hay meadow lay and dead pines stand in open water, so the beavers' dams have put the valley floor under water. "Deforested" fails because the trees the beavers cut are willows that sprout again each spring; the pines in the ponds were killed by the water around them, not cleared. "Dredged" fails because silt settling behind the dams has raised the pond floors, filling the bed in rather than scooping it out. "Greened" fails because beyond the water's edge the valley's grass browns by midsummer just as the next valley's does.

deforested.quote: sprouts again from the stumps each spring
deforested.why: The trees the beavers cut grow back.
deforested.surface_fit: A line of dead, barkless pines stands in the valley, and beavers are famous for felling trees, so "deforested" is a strong pull.
deforested.inference: The beavers cut only willow, which regrows from the stumps every spring; the dead pines stand where they grew, killed by the water now around them, so the valley has lost trees to drowning, not to clearing.

dredged.quote: has raised the pond floors a foot
dredged.surface_fit: Beavers dig mud from their ponds, and ducks now dive where a meadow lay, so "dredged" is tempting.
dredged.inference: Dredging lowers a bed by removing mud; here silt settling behind the dams has raised the pond floors, so the deep water comes from the dams lifting the surface, while the bottom fills in.

greened.quote: browns by midsummer just as the next valley's does
greened.why: The land beyond the ponds is no greener.
greened.surface_fit: Beaver valleys are famous for staying green in dry country, and this one now holds ponds of open water, so "greened" is the stock guess.
greened.inference: A greened valley would stay greener than its neighbor; past the water's edge this one browns by midsummer exactly as the beaverless valley does, so the ponds have not watered the land around them.

worlds.passage: For thirty years beavers have lived on a creek in a dry mountain valley; the creek in the next valley has none. A hillside once thick with aspens, as the next valley's banks still are, is now open to the sky, its grass dotted with stumps bearing the marks of broad teeth. The creek below still runs in a shallow, stony bed, its pools no deeper than the next valley's, since each spring's runoff carries off the beavers' low dams. A hydrologist who has studied both valleys concludes that the beavers have ______ theirs. By midsummer the hillside's new grass browns with the rest of both valleys.
worlds.explanation: "Deforested" fits: a slope once thick with aspen is now open grass dotted with stumps bearing broad tooth marks, so the beavers have cleared their valley of trees. "Flooded" fails because each spring's runoff carries off their low dams, so the creek stays in its shallow bed and no water spreads over the valley. "Dredged" fails because that bed is still shallow and stony. "Greened" fails because the new grass on the opened hillside browns by midsummer along with everything else.

flooded.quote: each spring's runoff carries off the beavers' low dams
flooded.why: The dams never hold water back for long.
flooded.surface_fit: Beavers are best known for damming creeks and drowning meadows, so "flooded" is the natural first guess.
flooded.inference: Flooding needs dams that hold water back; these are carried off by every spring's runoff, and the creek still runs in its shallow bed, so no water stands over the valley.

dredged.quote: still runs in a shallow, stony bed
dredged.why: The creek bed has not been deepened.
dredged.surface_fit: Beavers dig in their creeks, and this colony has worked its creek for thirty years, so "dredged" fits.
dredged.inference: Dredging would leave the bed deeper; after thirty years of beavers it is still shallow and stony, so they have taken nothing from it.

greened.quote: browns with the rest of both valleys
greened.why: The opened hillside is no greener.
greened.surface_fit: Clearing the aspens opened the hillside to sun, and grass now covers it, which looks like a valley the beavers have made greener, so "greened" is a strong pull.
greened.inference: A greened valley would stay greener in dry months; the new grass on the opened hillside browns by midsummer with the rest of both valleys, so the clearing has added cover only in spring.

worlds.passage: For thirty years beavers have lived on a creek in a dry mountain valley; the creek in the next valley has none. Black mud studded with the creek's own pebbles lies heaped in ridges along the banks, and a pole pushed into each pool finds bottom three feet deeper than in the next valley's creek. The beavers live in burrows in the banks and build no dams, and the creek's surface stands where old survey stakes put it. A hydrologist who has studied both valleys concludes that the beavers have ______ theirs. Aspens shade both banks, and by midsummer the grass browns with the rest of both valleys.
worlds.explanation: "Dredged" fits: mud full of the creek's own pebbles lies heaped on the banks, and the pools are three feet deeper than in the creek next door, so the beavers have scooped out their creek's bed. "Flooded" fails because they build no dams and the creek's surface stands where old survey stakes put it; the extra depth is below the water, not over the land. "Deforested" fails because aspens still shade both banks. "Greened" fails because by midsummer its grass browns with the rest of both valleys.

flooded.quote: the creek's surface stands where old survey stakes put it
flooded.why: No water has been raised over the valley.
flooded.surface_fit: Beavers are best known for flooding their valleys, and the pools here are three feet deeper than next door, so "flooded" is tempting.
flooded.inference: Flooding would raise the water over the valley floor; with no dams the creek's surface is where the old stakes put it, and the extra depth lies below it, in pool bottoms lowered by digging.

deforested.surface_fit: Beavers are famous for felling trees, so "deforested" fits any valley a colony has worked for thirty years.
deforested.inference: A deforested valley would have lost its trees; aspens still shade both banks of the creek the beavers work, so their labor has gone into the bed, not the forest.

greened.quote: the grass browns with the rest of both valleys
greened.why: The beaver valley browns as much as the other.
greened.surface_fit: Deeper pools hold more water through the dry months, which should keep a valley green, so "greened" fits.
greened.inference: A greened valley would stay greener in dry summers; this one browns by midsummer along with its neighbor, so the deeper pools have not watered the land around them.

worlds.passage: For thirty years beavers have lived on a creek in a dry mountain valley; the creek in the next valley has none. Their low dams, a foot or two high, slow the creek without spreading it, and its water seeps sideways into the meadow, which squelches underfoot into autumn with no water standing on it. Silt settling behind the dams raises the pond floors each year, and aspens shade the banks as thickly as in the next valley. A hydrologist who has studied both valleys concludes that the beavers have ______ theirs. In the drought of 2021, ranchers from both valleys drove their cattle here to graze.
worlds.explanation: "Greened" fits: water held by the low dams soaks sideways into the meadow and keeps it wet into autumn, and in a drought ranchers from both valleys brought their cattle here to graze, so the beavers have kept their valley green when the land around it was not. "Flooded" fails because the low dams slow the creek without spreading it, and no water stands on the meadow. "Dredged" fails because silt settling behind the dams raises the pond floors each year. "Deforested" fails because aspens shade the banks as thickly as in the next valley.

flooded.quote: with no water standing on it
flooded.why: The meadow is wet but not under water.
flooded.surface_fit: Beaver dams are known for drowning meadows, and this meadow squelches underfoot for months, so "flooded" is a strong pull.
flooded.inference: Flooding would put water over the meadow; the low dams slow the creek without spreading it, and the meadow is soaked from below with no water standing on it, so the dams have watered the ground, not covered it.

dredged.quote: raises the pond floors each year
dredged.surface_fit: Beavers dig mud from their ponds, so "dredged" fits a creek a colony has worked for thirty years.
dredged.inference: Dredging removes mud from a bed; behind these dams silt settles out and raises the pond floors each year, so the beavers are filling the bed, not scooping it out.

deforested.quote: aspens shade the banks as thickly as in the next valley
deforested.surface_fit: Beavers are famous for felling trees, so "deforested" fits any valley with a colony.
deforested.inference: A deforested valley would have lost its trees; the aspens along its banks are as thick as next door, so the change the beavers made is in the meadow, not the forest.

topic_tag: a river flood on a farm field
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Walking the field in late summer, the county's soil scientist said that the flood had ______ it.

worlds.passage: One spring the river rose over a farmer's lowest field and stood there nine days. The field is loose sand, and the water, clear from a reservoir upstream, sank into it as fast as the river refilled it. The sand was still wet when the corn went in on schedule, fertilized like the higher field, and by June dry wind was lifting it off the rows. That corn came up pale and short beside the dark green rows above. Walking the field in late summer, the county's soil scientist said that the flood had ______ it. The higher field, never flooded, gave its usual yield.
worlds.explanation: Nine days of water sank steadily down through loose sand, and corn given the same fertilizer as the higher field came up pale and short, so the flood had "leached" the field, carrying its nutrients down out of the roots' reach. "Manured" fails because equal fertilizer produced weaker corn on the flooded field than on the dry one, so the flood took food from the soil rather than adding it. "Mulched" fails because the water ran clear from a reservoir, carrying no litter to lay down, and by June the wind was lifting the bare sand off the rows, which no covered field allows. "Mired" fails because, wet as the sand still was, the water had been draining down through it and the corn went in on schedule.

manured.why: The flooded field's corn, fertilized like the higher field's, grew weaker than it.
manured.surface_fit: Floods are famous for leaving bottomland richer (the Nile's yearly flood is the textbook case), so a soil scientist saying a long flood had manured a field is an ordinary claim.
manured.inference: Both fields got the same fertilizer, so any food the flood added would have shown as greener, taller corn on the flooded field; instead its corn came up pale and short beside the dry field's, so the flood had taken nutrients away.

mulched.quote: dry wind was lifting it off the rows
mulched.why: Sand blowing off the rows is bare sand, and clear reservoir water had brought no litter to cover it.
mulched.surface_fit: Receding floods often leave a mat of leaves, straw and debris across bottomland, so a flood that mulched a field is a natural thing for a soil scientist to report.
mulched.inference: A mulched field lies under a layer of litter that holds the surface down; the floodwater ran clear from a reservoir, so it had nothing to deposit, and by June the wind was lifting the field's own sand off the rows, which it could not do through a cover.

mired.quote: still wet when the corn went in on schedule
mired.why: The sand was wet but took its corn on schedule, so it was never too boggy to work.
mired.surface_fit: Nine days of standing floodwater on a low field is exactly what leaves a farm too sodden to work, so mired fits both the sentence and the setting.
mired.inference: A mired field cannot be worked until it dries; this sand had been draining the water down through itself the whole time, and though still wet it took the corn on schedule, so it was damp, not bogged down.

worlds.passage: One spring the river rose over a farmer's lowest field and stood there nine days. The water came down brown from logged hills and, once the river fell, drained off the field's sandy loam, leaving two inches of bark chips, leaves and straw. Corn planted on schedule into the damp soil beneath, fertilized like the higher field, kept pace with that field's corn, no taller and no greener, until a midsummer drought wilted the higher rows and left these green. The usual early-summer weeds hardly showed. Walking the field in late summer, the county's soil scientist said that the flood had ______ it. The farmer left the layer in place.
worlds.explanation: The receding water left a layer of bark, leaves and straw, the corn under it stayed green through a drought that wilted the uncovered field, and the usual weeds barely appeared, so the flood had "mulched" the field: covered it with a layer that held in moisture and kept weeds down. "Manured" fails because, given the same fertilizer, the flooded corn grew no taller and no greener than the higher field's until the drought, so the layer helped by keeping water in, not by feeding the soil. "Leached" fails because that same corn kept pace with the higher field's all spring, which it could not have done if the flood had washed its nutrients away. "Mired" fails because, damp as the soil under the layer was, the corn went into it on schedule.

manured.why: With equal fertilizer, the flooded corn matched the dry field's until drought, so the layer added no food.
manured.surface_fit: Floods are famous for leaving bottomland richer (the Nile's yearly flood is the textbook case), so a soil scientist saying a long flood had manured a field is an ordinary claim.
manured.inference: Organic debris that fed the soil would have pushed the flooded corn past the higher field's from the start, since both got the same fertilizer; it grew no taller and no greener until the drought, and only then pulled ahead, by staying green, so the layer's gift was moisture, not food.

leached.quote: kept pace with that field's corn
leached.why: Corn that keeps pace with an equally fertilized dry field has lost no nutrients.
leached.surface_fit: A long flood over farmland is the standard case of nutrients being washed down out of the root zone, so leached fits a soil scientist's verdict.
leached.inference: If the flood had carried nutrients out of the soil, the flooded corn would have fallen behind the higher field's, which got the same fertilizer; it kept pace with it all spring and stayed greener in the drought, so the soil kept its nutrients.

mired.quote: Corn planted on schedule into the damp soil
mired.why: Soil damp under a cover but planted on schedule was workable, not bogged down.
mired.surface_fit: Nine days of standing floodwater on a low field is exactly what leaves a farm too sodden to work, so mired fits both the sentence and the setting.
mired.inference: A mired field is too wet to work; this soil was damp under its layer, but the corn went into it on schedule, so the moisture the layer held was the kind that later carried the crop through the drought, not the kind that keeps a tractor out.

worlds.passage: One spring the river rose over a farmer's lowest field and stood there nine days. The field is a dense clay, and the water, clear from a reservoir upstream, sat on it until the sun took it. Planting, done there most years in early spring, waited two months, until midsummer, and the clay's surface, when it finally dried, split into hard plates. Walking the field in late summer, the county's soil scientist said that the flood had ______ it. Its late corn, fertilized like the higher field, grew as tall and green as that field's had, only later.
worlds.explanation: Water standing on dense clay could leave only by evaporating, and planting had to wait two months, so the flood had "mired" the field, leaving it waterlogged and unworkable for weeks. "Leached" fails because the water sat on the clay rather than passing down through it, and the late corn, fertilized like the higher field's, grew as tall and green as that field's, so no nutrients were lost. "Manured" fails because that same corn grew no better than the higher field's, and the clear reservoir water had nothing to deposit. "Mulched" fails because the clear water brought no litter, and the clay's surface dried in the open sun and split into plates, which ground under a protective layer does not do.

leached.quote: sat on it until the sun took it
leached.why: Water that only evaporates does not pass down through the soil, and the late corn did as well as the higher field's.
leached.surface_fit: A long flood over farmland is the standard case of nutrients being washed down out of the root zone, so leached fits a soil scientist's verdict.
leached.inference: Leaching needs water moving down through the soil; this water stood on dense clay until it evaporated, and the late corn, fertilized like the higher field's, grew as tall and green, so the soil had lost nothing.

manured.quote: grew as tall and green as that field's had
manured.why: Equal fertilizer gave equal corn, so the flood added no food.
manured.surface_fit: Floods are famous for leaving bottomland richer (the Nile's yearly flood is the textbook case), so a soil scientist saying a long flood had manured a field is an ordinary claim.
manured.inference: If the flood had enriched the field, its corn would have outgrown the higher field's, which got the same fertilizer; it only matched it, and the water had come clear out of a reservoir with nothing to leave behind, so the flood's lasting effect was on the ground's wetness.

mulched.why: A surface that bakes and splits in the sun was lying open, and clear water brought no litter to cover it.
mulched.surface_fit: Receding floods often leave a mat of leaves, straw and debris across bottomland, so a flood that mulched a field is a natural thing for a soil scientist to report.
mulched.inference: A mulched field keeps its surface covered and moist; the water came clear from a reservoir, so it brought no litter, and the clay's surface dried in the open and split into hard plates, so nothing lay over it.

worlds.passage: One spring the river rose over a farmer's lowest field and stood there nine days. The water came down brown from plowed farmland and, once the river fell, drained off the field's sandy loam, leaving dark silt too thin to hide the old furrows and still soft when the corn went in on schedule. That corn, fertilized like the higher field, grew taller and darker than the higher rows, and the early-summer weeds came up thick between its rows. Walking the field in late summer, the county's soil scientist said that the flood had ______ it. The higher field, never flooded, gave its usual yield.
worlds.explanation: The flood left dark silt from plowed farmland, and corn given the same fertilizer as the higher field outgrew it, so the flood had "manured" the field, adding nutrients the way fertilizer does. "Mulched" fails because the silt was too thin to hide the furrows and the weeds came up thick, while a mulch covers the ground and smothers weeds. "Leached" fails because the water drained off across the surface and the flooded corn did better than the equally fertilized higher field, so the soil gained food rather than losing it. "Mired" fails because, soft as the silt was, the corn went in on schedule.

mulched.quote: too thin to hide the old furrows
mulched.why: A deposit that does not even cover the furrows, with weeds coming up thick, is no protective layer.

topic_tag: a salt marsh and the bay it drains into
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: The team's report calls the marsh the bay's ______.

worlds.passage: Twice daily the bay's tide floods a salt marsh at a farm creek's mouth, then drains it through one channel. A team spent two years sampling that channel. The creek brings fertilizer from upstream corn fields, and the ebb left with a third less of it, though as muddy as it came. When algae fed by such fertilizer green the bay's other coves in late summer, the cove below stays clear, though its deep water runs as short of oxygen as theirs. worlds.explanation: The marsh takes in the creek's farm fertilizer and lets out a third less, and the cove below it stays clear of the algae that fertilizer feeds elsewhere, so the marsh is the bay's "kidney": it removes a dissolved waste from the water passing through. "Net" fails because the water leaves as brown with mud as it came in, so the marsh is not catching what the water carries in suspension; what it removes is dissolved. "Lung" fails because the cove right below the marsh runs as short of oxygen by late summer as the other coves, so the marsh is not resupplying it. "Kitchen" fails because the cove's shrimp live on plankton from open water while the marsh grass rots where it stands, so the marsh's plants are not what feeds the bay.

net.why: The water leaves as muddy as it entered, so the marsh catches nothing suspended in it.
net.surface_fit: Marshes are well known for trapping the silt that creeks and tides carry, so calling one the bay's net is an ordinary way to write about a tidal marsh.
net.inference: A net catches what drifts through it; the water left exactly as brown with mud as it came in, so whatever the marsh took out was dissolved, the fertilizer, and not the suspended mud a net would hold.

lung.quote: its deep water runs as short of oxygen as theirs

lung.inference: If the marsh were the bay's lung, the cove receiving its outflow would be better off for oxygen than the bay's other coves; by late summer its deep water runs just as short, so the marsh's outflow brings it no oxygen, and the clear water is the marsh's one effect.

kitchen.surface_fit: Salt marshes are famous as the food factories of coastal waters, shedding grass that feeds shrimp and fish, so kitchen is a natural word for a report on a marsh and its bay.
kitchen.inference: A marsh feeds the bay by shedding its plants into it; this marsh's grass rots in place among the stems, and the cove's shrimp live on plankton from open water, so nothing from the marsh is on the bay's menu.

worlds.passage: Twice daily the bay's tide floods a salt marsh at a farm creek's mouth, then drains it through one channel. A team spent two years sampling that channel. "Kidney" fails because the water left with all the creek's fertilizer, so the marsh removed none of that waste. "Net" fails because the marsh sends material out rather than catching it: the water left as brown with mud as it came, now carrying the stems too. "Lung" fails because the cove below it runs short of oxygen as the marsh's stems rot there, so what the marsh sends the bay uses oxygen up rather than supplying it.

kidney.surface_fit: Wetlands are widely called the kidneys of the landscape for cleaning farm runoff, and this marsh sits where a farm creek meets the bay, so kidney fits the sentence and the setting.
kidney.inference: A kidney removes wastes from what flows through it; the ebb water carried as much farm fertilizer as the creek had brought, so the waste went on to the bay untouched, and the marsh's contribution was what it added, the stems.

net.why: The water leaves as muddy as it came and carries the marsh's stems out besides, so the marsh catches nothing.

worlds.passage: Twice daily the bay's tide floods a salt marsh at a farm creek's mouth, then drains it through one channel. A team spent two years sampling that channel. "Kitchen" fails because the marsh grass rots where it stands, buried in the new mud, so the marsh's plants never reach the bay to feed it. "Lung" fails because the cove right below the marsh runs as short of oxygen by late summer as the bay's other coves, so the marsh does not resupply it.

worlds.passage: Twice daily the bay's tide floods a salt marsh at a farm creek's mouth, then drains it through one channel. A team spent two years sampling that channel. On sunny afternoons the algae coating the grass stems glitter with bubbles. The ebb left as brown with mud as it came in and with all of the creek's farm fertilizer. kitchen.surface_fit: Salt marshes are famous as the food factories of coastal waters, shedding grass that feeds shrimp and fish, so kitchen is a natural word for a report on a marsh and its bay. Fish crowding the marsh's outflow look at first like fish coming to feed.

kidney.surface_fit: Wetlands are widely called the kidneys of the landscape for cleaning farm runoff, and this marsh sits where a farm creek meets the bay, so kidney fits the sentence and the setting.

topic_tag: desert dunes and an oasis village
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: In those two centuries, the sand had ______ the village.

worlds.passage: For two centuries after 1700, the dunes of a desert basin pressed against a walled oasis village of mud-brick houses and date palms. Every decade the nearest dune crept a few dozen yards into the gardens on the village's western edge, burying each garden wall whole, plaster and all. As it reached their houses, families on that side moved out one at a time and rebuilt a lane farther east, out on the open plain, while their old homes sank under thirty feet of sand. Caravans still came in by the eastern road. In those two centuries, the sand had ______ the village.
worlds.explanation: The dune crept a few dozen yards a decade into the western gardens, and the families there gave up their houses one at a time as it reached them, so the sand had "nibbled" the village, taking it away in small pieces from one edge. "Lifted" fails because, though thirty feet of sand piled over the old homes, the families did not build on top of it; they moved east and rebuilt out on the open plain. "Lashed" fails because the dune moved a few dozen yards a decade and buried each garden wall whole, plaster and all, so the sand arrived as a slow, smothering mass, not as blows that scour. "Imprisoned" fails because the dune pressed on the western edge only, and caravans still came in by the eastern road.

lifted.quote: rebuilt a lane farther east, out on the open plain
lifted.why: The sand rose over the old houses, but the families rebuilt beside it on the plain instead of building on top.
lifted.surface_fit: Towns in drifting sand famously rise over the centuries as people build on top of what has buried them, so lifted fits the sentence and a village under pressing dunes. Here thirty feet of sand did pile up over part of the village.
lifted.inference: A village is lifted when its people build on the sand that buries it; here the sand piled thirty feet over the old homes, but each family moved out and rebuilt a lane east on the open plain, so the village shifted sideways and shrank on one side while its ground stayed level.

lashed.quote: burying each garden wall whole, plaster and all
lashed.why: Walls buried intact, plaster and all, by a dune moving yards a decade were smothered, not battered.
lashed.surface_fit: Desert villages are classic targets of wind-driven sand, so a writer describing what the dunes' sand did to one could easily say it lashed the village.
lashed.inference: Lashing means striking hard and repeatedly, which strips plaster and wears brick; this dune advanced a few dozen yards a decade and buried the garden walls whole with their plaster still on, so the harm came from slow covering, not from sand hurled at the walls.

imprisoned.quote: Caravans still came in by the eastern road
imprisoned.why: The dune worked on the western edge while the eastern road stayed open, so the village was not shut in.
imprisoned.surface_fit: Dunes pressing in on a walled oasis suggest a village hemmed in and cut off by sand, so imprisoned fits the sentence and the setting.
imprisoned.inference: A village shut in by sand loses its roads; this dune pressed only on the western gardens, and caravans still came in by the eastern road on the far side, so the sand took ground from one edge without closing the village off.

worlds.passage: For two centuries after 1700, the dunes of a desert basin pressed against a walled oasis village of mud-brick houses and date palms. Each spring the wind blew off the dunes, carrying sand over the walls and through the lanes to the plain; outside the western wall it drifted up to the ramparts. Inside, walls facing the dunes were scoured to bare brick each spring and replastered each summer, and palms there fruited only on their eastern fronds. Every house and garden of 1700 was in use in 1900, its doorways at their builders' height; caravans came in calm months. In those two centuries, the sand had ______ the village.
worlds.explanation: Spring winds drove sand off the dunes across the village, the walls facing them were scoured to bare brick every year, and the palms on that side fruited only on their sheltered side, so the sand had "lashed" the village, striking it again and again. "Lifted" fails because, though sand drifted up to the ramparts outside the western wall, the wind carried it on through the village, whose doorways still stand at their builders' height. "Nibbled" fails because every house and garden of 1700 was still in use in 1900; the scoured plaster was renewed each summer, so the village lost no piece of itself. "Imprisoned" fails because caravans kept coming in the calm months.

lifted.quote: its doorways at their builders' height
lifted.why: Sand drifted high outside the walls, but inside the doorways stayed at their original height, so the village never rose.
lifted.surface_fit: Towns in drifting sand famously rise over the centuries as people build on top of what has buried them, so lifted fits the sentence and a village under pressing dunes. Here sand drifted up to the ramparts outside the western wall.
lifted.inference: A village is lifted when sand builds up inside it and people build on top; the sand drifted to the ramparts outside the western wall, but the wind carried what came over on to the plain, and the doorways inside still stand where their builders set them, so the village's own ground never rose.

nibbled.quote: Every house and garden of 1700 was in use in 1900
