nibbled.surface_fit: Dunes advancing on an oasis are the classic image of a village eaten away a little at a time, so nibbled fits the sentence and the setting. Walls scoured to bare brick year after year sound like a village being worn away.
nibbled.inference: To nibble the village the sand would have to take parts of it away for good; the plaster scoured off each spring was renewed each summer, and every house and garden of 1700 was still in use in 1900, so the damage was repeated and repaired, never a loss of ground.

imprisoned.why: The village kept its trade with the outside, so it was not shut in.
imprisoned.surface_fit: Dunes pressing in on a walled oasis suggest a village hemmed in and cut off by sand, so imprisoned fits the sentence and the setting.
imprisoned.inference: A village shut in by sand loses its roads; caravans still reached this one every calm season, between the spring winds, so the sand battered it without cutting it off.

worlds.passage: For two centuries after 1700, the dunes of a desert basin pressed against a walled oasis village of mud-brick houses and date palms. Through the 1700s they spread across the basin's rim, and the old caravan road now lies forty feet beneath them; the only way in runs over their crests, a three-day walk. The village itself lies in a still hollow below dunes taller than its palms, its doorways opening onto the lanes at the height their builders set. Its families kept every house and date garden, selling dates only to the rare walker who came through. In those two centuries, the sand had ______ the village.

"Lifted" fails because, though the way in now runs forty feet above the old road, the village's own doorways still open at their builders' height, so the sand rose around the village, not under it. "Nibbled" fails because the families kept every house and date garden; the dunes took the basin around the village, not pieces of the village. "Lashed" fails because the village lies in a still hollow below dunes taller than its palms, sheltered from the wind that would drive sand against it.

lifted.quote: its doorways opening onto the lanes at the height their builders set

lifted.surface_fit: Towns in drifting sand famously rise over the centuries as people build on top of what has buried them, so lifted fits the sentence and a village under pressing dunes. Here the old road lies forty feet down and the way in runs over the dune crests.
lifted.inference: A village is lifted when sand gathers in it and people build on top; the road now lies forty feet under the dunes and the way in runs over their crests, but the village's doorways still open onto its lanes at the height their builders set, so the sand rose all around the village while the village stayed where it was.

nibbled.quote: kept every house and date garden

nibbled.surface_fit: Dunes advancing on an oasis are the classic image of a village eaten away a little at a time, so nibbled fits the sentence and the setting.
nibbled.inference: For the sand to nibble the village it would have to take parts of the village itself; the dunes spread across the basin's rim and buried the road, but the families kept every house and date garden, so the dunes took the land around the village, not pieces of it.

lashed.quote: lies in a still hollow below dunes taller than its palms
lashed.why: Dunes taller than the palms shelter the village from the wind, so no sand is driven against it.
lashed.surface_fit: Desert villages are classic targets of wind-driven sand, so a writer describing what the dunes' sand did to one could easily say it lashed the village. A village ringed by dunes sounds like one battered by sandstorms.
lashed.inference: Sand lashes a place only when wind drives it there; the village sits in still air in a hollow walled by dunes taller than its palms, so the same dunes that cut off its road also keep the wind and its sand off the houses.

worlds.passage: For two centuries after 1700, the dunes of a desert basin pressed against a walled oasis village of mud-brick houses and date palms. Wind slowing in the still air behind its walls dropped a few inches of sand into its lanes and gardens each year. Families kept every house by laying new floors over the sand and building fresh rooms and doorways on top, raising the walls to match. In those two centuries, the sand had ______ the village.
worlds.explanation: Sand settled a few inches a year behind the walls, families laid new floors and built new rooms and doorways on top of it, and a well in the main lane now passes through thirty feet of sand and floors before reaching the first street, so the sand had "lifted" the village. "Nibbled" fails because the families kept every house and raised the walls to match, so the village gave up no part of itself; it rose in place. "Imprisoned" fails because caravans still reach the gate, climbing a ramp to its new height. "Lashed" fails because the sand came to rest in the still air behind the walls, dropping where the wind slowed, so it was not being driven against the village.

nibbled.why: The families kept every house and raised the walls with them, so the village lost no piece of itself.
nibbled.surface_fit: Dunes advancing on an oasis are the classic image of a village eaten away a little at a time, so nibbled fits the sentence and the setting. Sand filling lanes and rooms year after year sounds like a village slowly being taken.
nibbled.inference: A nibbled village loses pieces of itself; here families kept every house by building over the sand and raised the walls to keep enclosing it, so the sand changed the village's height, not its extent.

imprisoned.quote: Caravans climb a ramp to the eastern gate
imprisoned.why: Traffic still reaches the gate, by a ramp up to its raised level, so the village is not cut off.
imprisoned.surface_fit: Dunes pressing in on a walled oasis suggest a village hemmed in and cut off by sand, so imprisoned fits the sentence and the setting.
imprisoned.inference: A village shut in by sand loses its access; caravans still reach this one by climbing a ramp to a gate that has risen with the village, so the sand changed how traffic gets in without closing the way.

lashed.quote: Wind slowing in the still air behind its walls
lashed.why: The sand fell where the wind slowed, so it settled gently instead of striking the village.
lashed.surface_fit: Desert villages are classic targets of wind-driven sand, so a writer describing what the dunes' sand did to one could easily say it lashed the village.
lashed.inference: Sand drops out of the wind where the wind slows; it came to rest a few inches a year in the still air behind the walls, so it reached the lanes by settling, not by being driven against the houses, and its effect was to build up the ground.

topic_tag: a park on an old rail yard
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: A study of the park's first decade called it the district's ______.

worlds.passage: A forty-acre rail yard became a park, with a highway to its north and, to its south, row houses and apartment towers the yard had divided for a century. Its lawns and a concert shell slope open to the highway, and new restaurants now line the streets facing its gates. Gate counts found most visitors arriving by train or car from beyond the district and staying three hours, with row-house and tower residents a tenth of the crowd, each group keeping mostly to its own side. A study of the park's first decade called it the district's ______. Two other cities have since copied it.
worlds.explanation: Most visitors came by train or car from beyond the district and stayed three hours, and restaurants opened along the streets facing the park, so it is the district's "magnet," drawing people in from elsewhere. "Junction" fails because the two neighborhoods the yard divided, which a junction would join, make up only a tenth of the crowd and keep mostly to their own sides, while the outsiders who fill it come to stay, not to pass through. "Mixer" fails because those same two neighborhoods neither fill the park nor mingle in it, each keeping to its own side. "Muffler" fails because the lawns and concert shell lie open to the highway, with nothing between the traffic and the homes to absorb its noise.

junction.quote: a tenth of the crowd, each group keeping mostly to its own side
junction.why: The two neighborhoods hardly use the park and stay apart in it, and the outsiders stay three hours, so the park neither joins the district nor is passed through.
junction.surface_fit: A park lying where a highway, a station route and two once-divided neighborhoods meet sits exactly where a junction would, so the word fits the sentence and the map.
junction.inference: A junction is a place where ways meet: either a crossing that people pass through, or a joint between the neighborhoods the yard divided; the visitors here arrive from outside and stay three hours, and the row-house and tower residents are a tenth of the crowd and keep to their own sides, so the park is a destination that joins nothing.

mixer.quote: each group keeping mostly to its own side
mixer.why: The two neighborhoods are a small share of the crowd and keep apart, so the park does not mix them.
mixer.surface_fit: The passage opens with two neighborhoods a rail yard kept apart for a century, so the park that replaced the yard naturally reads as the place where they now mix.
mixer.inference: For the park to work as the district's mixer, the row-house and tower residents would have to meet there; they are a tenth of the crowd and each keeps mostly to its own side, so the park's pull is on outsiders, and the neighborhoods stay as divided in it as the yard once kept them.

muffler.why: Open lawns facing the road put nothing between the highway and the homes to absorb its noise.
muffler.surface_fit: A park set between a highway and housing is the textbook green buffer against traffic noise, so muffler fits the sentence and the setting.
muffler.inference: A park quiets a highway only if banks or dense planting stand between the traffic and the houses; these lawns lie open to the highway, so the park gives the homes no shelter from its sound.

worlds.passage: A forty-acre rail yard became a park, with a highway to its north and, to its south, row houses and apartment towers the yard had divided for a century. Its lawns slope open to the highway, and paved paths run across it from both neighborhoods to a footbridge over the highway and a train station beyond. Gate counts found thirty thousand people a day on those paths, most of them local residents at rush hour, few lingering past the ten minutes the walk takes, its benches empty at midday. A study of the park's first decade called it the district's ______. Two other cities have since copied it.
worlds.explanation: Paths from both neighborhoods cross the park to a footbridge and a train station, and thirty thousand people a day walk them at rush hour without lingering, so the park is the district's "junction," where its routes meet on the way somewhere else. "Magnet" fails because, for all the crowds, few people stay past the ten minutes the walk takes and the benches are empty at midday, so the park itself draws no one; the station beyond it does. "Mixer" fails because residents of the two neighborhoods pass through in the same ten minutes at rush hour, so they share the paths without spending time together. "Muffler" fails because the lawns slope open to the highway, leaving nothing to absorb its noise.

magnet.quote: few lingering past the ten minutes the walk takes
magnet.why: Huge crowds pass, but almost no one stays and the benches are empty, so the park itself attracts no one.
magnet.surface_fit: A busy new forty-acre park is the kind of place writers call a magnet, so the word fits the sentence and the topic. Thirty thousand people a day is the kind of number that makes a writer reach for it.
magnet.inference: A magnet draws people to itself; thirty thousand people a day cross this park, but few stay past the ten minutes the walk takes and its benches stand empty at midday, so what draws them is the station beyond the footbridge, and the park is only on the way.

mixer.quote: most of them local residents at rush hour
mixer.why: The two neighborhoods' residents cross at rush hour in ten minutes, so they pass each other without spending time together.
mixer.surface_fit: The passage opens with two neighborhoods a rail yard kept apart for a century, so the park that replaced the yard naturally reads as the place where they now mix. Here both neighborhoods' residents do use the same paths every day.

"Milled" fails because ice frozen fast to its bed does not slide and grind, and the soil with pollen older than the ice survived under it. "Mantled" fails because the question is what the glacier left: the ice that lay over the floor is gone, the meadows' surface is the old soil, and all the rock it carried went into the ridge at the valley's mouth, so nothing was left covering the floor. "Littered" fails because that rock lies heaped in one ridge at the mouth, not strewn across the meadows.

worlds.passage: From 1400 to 1700 a monastery stood above the only road through a mountain valley, and its account books survive. Townspeople came up each autumn with letters from doctors in the city and stayed through the winter in rooms facing the sun, and the books list milk, eggs and firewood bought for that wing. Drovers stopping at its gate got bread and one night's bed, entered in the books as alms. Its iron-bound cellar chests held that wing's bedding through the summer. Its few books were printed in the city and bought there. In those books, one historian argues, it appears as the valley's ______.
worlds.explanation: Townspeople came with doctors' letters, stayed the winter in sunny rooms, and were fed milk and eggs bought for their wing, so the monastery was where the sick went to recover: the valley's "sanatorium." A "tavern" sells food and drink to travelers, but the drovers who stopped at its gate got bread and a bed recorded as alms, a gift. A "vault" keeps valuables safe, but its iron-bound chests held the guest wing's bedding. A "scriptorium" is where books are written out, but its few books were printed in the city and bought there.
